By having his narrator defend this space as a site of intellectual privilege, Samuel Johnson does not simply write a light satire on the literary life; he investigates the relationship between material conditions and mental work, mocking the classical idea that the mind can achieve independence from the body and the environment by a simple act of elevation.
## The Geography of Grub Street

The paper does not present itself as a documentary account of Johnson's career or of London lodging. Its speaker adopts the borrowed name Hypertatus and turns the garret into a subject for mock scholarship. The joke depends on the distance between the grand explanations he offers and the ordinary room those explanations are meant to dignify.

That distance matters because the paper repeatedly makes a literary convention literal. Classical mountains, elevated dwellings, rarefied air, and the language of intellectual ascent are gathered into a single comic theory. The garret is therefore less a biographical fact than a device for testing how easily prestige can be manufactured by rhetoric.

Hypertatus, however, has transformed this setting into a philosophical temple. He lists the historical precedents for his elevation, citing the philosophers, astronomers, and poets who sought out high places for their work:

> "I have found by experience that the mind of man is modified by the place of his dwelling, and that elevation of site has a natural tendency to produce elevation of thought. The philosophers of antiquity did not study in cellars or valleys, but sought out the highest hills, that they might be closer to the stars and free from the distraction of the crowd."

The humor is in the literalness of the connection. Hypertatus argues that the thin air of the garret is superior for the production of light, airy thoughts, whereas the heavy air of cellars produces only dull, material ideas: "It is certain that the density of the air in low places has a depressing effect on the animal spirits; the writer who sits in a basement will always write in a heavy, pedantic style."
## The Satire of Philosophical Elevation

The critique of this "elevation of thought" is directed first at the theory itself. Hypertatus treats figurative associations between height and intelligence as if they were physical laws, and the paper lets the reader watch that mistake become more elaborate with every paragraph.

Johnson was deeply skeptical of any philosophy that claimed to make the mind independent of the body. Throughout his essays, he insisted on the physical limits of human life: we are subject to hunger, cold, disease, and the passage of time, and our moral decisions are always constrained by these realities. The sage who pretends to be indifferent to his environment is a fraud or a fool.
Hypertatus's description of his life in the garret reveals these limits, even as he tries to hide them under philosophical terms:

> "In this room, which is the highest in the house, I sit above the noise and distraction of the street. The cries of the fishmongers, the rattling of the coaches, and the disputes of the coal-carters do not reach me here. I am like the god of Epicurus, who looks down on the world without being disturbed by its changes."

The paper's material counterweight is not a narrated hardship but the body and the atmosphere. Hypertatus claims that air, motion, altitude, and even the earth's rotation alter intellectual powers. His proposed barometrical science turns the language of mental elevation into an absurdly measurable system, exposing the desire to give vanity the authority of experiment.

The paper's final joke extends the same logic to literary judgement. Hypertatus claims that the height of an author's dwelling can be inferred from the quality of the writing, then signs the letter before the theory can become a genuine system. The philosopher who has raised himself above ordinary measures ends by making his own pretension the measure of the joke.
## The Class Structure of the Lodging House

The lodging house in "The Garret" supplies a vertical diagram for the argument, but the paper does not require that diagram to stand as a social survey. Hypertatus turns floors and stories into intellectual categories:

> "The house in which I live is divided into different zones, according to the wealth and status of the tenants. The ground floor is occupied by a merchant, who is always busy and noisy; the first floor by a gentleman of fashion, who sleeps all day and stays out all night; the second floor by a family of quiet, industrious tradespeople; and the garret by myself."

Hypertatus's attempt to invert this hierarchy is a comic defence of elevation. He makes the upper room the seat of intellectual honour and turns ordinary spatial difference into a theory of mental capacity. The manoeuvre is persuasive only while the reader accepts the terms he has invented.

The irony lies in the speaker's confidence, not in a separately narrated story of poverty. His claim that a change of elevation can produce wit is continually enlarged until the explanation defeats itself. The garret remains a room; the theory makes it a cosmology.
## The Prose of Weight and Balance

Formally, "The Garret" is a model of Johnson's prose style, which is often called "Johnsonian" because of its distinctive weight, balance, and Latinate vocabulary. Unlike the conversational style of Steele or the light grace of Addison, Johnson's sentences are built around parallel structures, balanced clauses, and abstract nouns.

This style is often criticized as heavy or pedantic, but in "The Garret," it performs a specific comic function. The weight of the language contrasts with the triviality and delusion of the narrator's claims: the balanced, Latinate clauses are used to defend the thin air of the roof and the history of high-dwelling writers. The style gives the narrator's illusions a fake gravity, making his eventual collapse into the physical reality of his room more comic.

Yet the weight of the prose also carries a real moral gravity. Even in his lightest satires, Johnson is always looking for the universal truth of the human condition. The narrator's delusion is not unique to writers; it is a version of the vanity that runs through all human life, the desire to escape the limits of our nature by some artificial elevation of our role or our circumstances.
## The Descent to the Street

The essay ends with Hypertatus's signature, not with a narrated descent or conversion. The letter stops at the point where its mock science has reached its most extravagant form. That open stop preserves the joke's central pressure: the theory never has to meet a final refutation because its excess has already exposed it.

Johnson's *Rambler* paper leaves the reader with a double impression. We laugh at Hypertatus's theories of thin air, planetary motion, and literary altitude, but we also recognise the serious human wish beneath them: to make circumstances answer to an account of one's own importance. The paper's form keeps that wish comic without reducing it to a single biographical case.

chapters.title: 19. Samuel Johnson: "On the Art of Flying"

content.value: Samuel Johnson

**Original title:** *The History of Rasselas, Prince of Abissinia*, Chapter VI  
**Date:** 1759 CE  
**Original language:** English  
**Country/tradition:** England  
**Period/movement:** The Enlightenment; mid-eighteenth-century philosophical tale  
**Genre:** Philosophical essay; allegorical tale; early science fiction

Among the artists drawn to the Happy Valley is a man eminent in the mechanical arts, whose engines serve both use and recreation. Rasselas visits him because he is interested in knowledge and hopes that what he learns may help him in the open world. The artist's project of flight becomes a test of that hope: it turns an abstract desire for escape into a practical experiment with bodies, air, and gravity.

This encounter is the pressure point of the episode known here as "On the Art of Flying," originally Chapter VI of Samuel Johnson's philosophical fable *Rasselas* (1759), and frequently anthologised as a standalone selection. The chapter moves from mechanical speculation to a conversation between the artist and Rasselas about the feasibility and consequences of flight. By focusing on the artist's confidence and eventual failure, Johnson investigates the limits of human ambition while also imagining how a new power might alter the security of cities and states.
## The Irony of the Leap
The climax of the essay is the inventor's attempt to fly, which is recorded with dry, physical realism:

> "The artist was, for a year, busy in his work; and, at the end of the year, came to Rasselas with wings on his shoulders. He went to the top of a promontory, and leaped into the air. He did not rise, but fell immediately into the lake below; where his wings, which were made of wood and feathers, kept him from sinking until the Prince's servants came and pulled him out."

The transition from the grand ambition of the year-long preparation to the immediate fall into the lake is a study in understatement. The artist does not soar like Icarus or die like a tragic hero. He falls, and the wings that fail in the air sustain him in the water until Rasselas draws him to land.

This comic resolution belongs to Johnson's larger inquiry into human projects. Throughout *Rasselas*, characters seek happiness, wisdom, and power through competing schemes. The fall into the lake gives that inquiry a physical form: desire and ingenuity do not guarantee mastery over the conditions in which action takes place. The return to the ground is comic, but it also exposes the limits of confidence detached from experience.
## The Warning of the Sky-War

What raises "On the Art of Flying" above simple comedy is the inventor's conversation with Rasselas before the attempt. Rasselas is enthusiastic about the project, imagining the pleasure of looking down on the world from above and traveling without the obstacles of mountains, rivers, and borders. The inventor, however, is anxious about the potential misuse of his invention:

> "If men were to fly, they would soon use their wings for war. A city could not be defended against an army that could descend from the clouds; the palace of the king, the cottage of the peasant, the storehouses of the merchant would all be open to destruction from above. I will not reveal the secret of my invention to the world, lest I should be the author of its ruin."

This warning is a thought experiment within a 1759 philosophical tale. Later readers can recognise in it a speculation about how flight might change the security of cities and states, but the chapter need not be treated as a literal prediction of modern warfare. Its immediate subject is the moral risk of giving ambitious people a new power before deciding how that power should be governed.

The warning is grounded in the tale's suspicion that ingenuity does not automatically produce virtue. The artist can imagine a technical solution without resolving the political and moral consequences of distributing it. Johnson therefore keeps invention and judgement in tension rather than presenting progress as a simple route to improvement.
## The Happy Valley and the Prison of Ease

The setting of the essay is also crucial to its meaning. The Happy Valley is a paradise of ease and luxury, surrounded by high mountains that prevent the inhabitants from leaving. The Prince Rasselas is bored by this perfection; he wants to see the world, to experience the variety of human life, and to find his own "choice of life."

The inventor's attempt to fly responds to this confinement. The sky appears to offer a route beyond the mountains, and flight becomes a way of imagining escape from a paradise that has become a prison. The project is therefore connected to Rasselas's desire to enter the wider world, even though the artist's motives are also shaped by curiosity and confidence in his own powers.

This context complicates the inventor's failure. His fall is not only a personal embarrassment; it is a setback for the hope that technology can dissolve every boundary. The valley remains a place from which Rasselas still wants to escape. The episode suggests that freedom cannot be secured by physical movement alone, because the restless mind carries its dissatisfaction with it.
## The Style of the Moral Fable

Formally, "On the Art of Flying" is a philosophical-tale episode, using a simple, stylised narrative to investigate a moral question. The language is balanced and economical, with little of the local detail that would belong to a realistic travel narrative. Rasselas is named, but the artist remains an unnamed figure, and the Happy Valley functions as a generalised symbolic landscape.

This abstraction is deliberate. Johnson is not trying to write a technical description of a flying machine or a realistic account of Abissinia. He creates a fable of human ambition in which the wings stand for an attempt to rise above ordinary limits. The mechanical details matter because they keep that allegory attached to the resistance of material conditions.

The symmetry of the dialogue is also a key feature of the style. The conversation between Rasselas and the inventor is organized as a series of balances: the prince's hope vs. the inventor's fear; the utility of travel vs. the danger of war; the beauty of the design vs. the weakness of the arm. This structure allows Johnson to present both sides of the question of progress without resolving them too quickly, showing that the desire for advancement and the fear of its consequences are both permanent parts of our intellectual condition.
## The Return to the Ground

The episode ends with the artist being drawn from the lake, half dead with terror and vexation. His wings have no use in the air but sustain him in the water. Johnson stops at that physical reversal rather than narrating a return to the workshop or a new programme of practical machines.

The reversal supplies the episode's qualified conclusion. The artist who imagined himself rising above the world is returned to the material conditions he had hoped to overcome. This is comic rather than tragic, but the comedy does not erase the seriousness of the experiment. It makes ambition answerable to the body and to the limits of the medium through which it acts.

The essay suggests that the true work of the intellect is not the pursuit of the impossible, but the management of the possible. We must accept the ground, accept the gravity that pulls us down, and find our happiness in the daily, useful work of the valley rather than in the dangerous, wet leaps from the cliff. The art of flying is a dream; the art of living in a world of gravity is the real task.

chapters.title: 20. Jean-Jacques Rousseau: "Discourse on the Origin and Basis of Inequality Among Men"

content.value: Jean-Jacques Rousseau

**Original title:** *Discours sur l'origine et les fondements de l'inégalité parmi les hommes* (Second Discourse)  
**Date:** 1755 CE  
**Original language:** French  
**Country/tradition:** France / Switzerland  
**Period/movement:** The Enlightenment; political philosophy; pre-Romanticism  
**Genre:** Philosophical essay; political treatise

"The first man who, having enclosed a piece of ground, bethought himself of saying *This is mine*, and found people simple enough to believe him, was the real founder of civil society." With this declaration, Jean-Jacques Rousseau begins the second part of his *Discourse on the Origin and Basis of Inequality Among Men* (1755). The sentence has the force of a historical myth. It does not describe a legal contract or a gradual economic development; it describes a sudden, arbitrary act of usurpation that was accepted through the simplicity of others.

This act of enclosure is the pressure point of the essay. Rousseau is writing in response to a essay competition set by the Academy of Dijon, which asked: "What is the origin of inequality among men, and is it authorized by natural law?" Rousseau's response was a radical challenge to the political theory of his day. Unlike Thomas Hobbes, who argued that the state of nature was a war of all against all and that the state was necessary to preserve life, and John Locke, who argued that private property was a natural right based on labor, Rousseau argues that private property is the source of all our crimes, wars, and miseries, and that civil society is a trick played by the rich on the poor to secure their stolen wealth.
## The Physicality of Natural Man

To understand how inequality arose, Rousseau begins by stripping away all the additions of civilization to reconstruct the "natural man." He describes a figure that is physically robust, solitary, and free from the anxieties of the modern mind:

> "I see him satisfying his hunger under an oak, quenching his thirst at the first brook, finding his bed at the foot of the same tree on which he has dined, and with that, all his wants are supplied."

Natural man has no language, no home, no family, and no concept of the future. He lives entirely in the present, his mind governed by two natural instincts: the desire for self-preservation (*amour de soi*) and a natural repugnance at the sight of another sentient being's suffering (*pitié* or pity).

This natural pity is the moral anchor of the essay. Rousseau argues that pity is not a social virtue learned from religion or philosophy, but a biological capacity that precedes all reason. It is what keeps the strong from exploiting the weak in the state of nature: "Pity is what, in the state of nature, takes the place of laws, morals, and virtue, with the advantage that no one is tempted to disobey its sweet voice."

Civilization, in Rousseau's account, works by suppressing this natural pity. By training us to think in terms of calculation, competition, and property, civil society isolates us from one another. The philosopher, looking out his window at a riot on the street, can close his eyes and argue himself into indifference: "He has only to say to himself, 'Perish if you will; I am secure.'"
## The Leap into Property and Division of Labor

The transition from this natural state to civil society is not a linear progress, but a series of accidents and technological changes. The key developments are the invention of metallurgy and agriculture:
> "To the poet, it is gold and silver, but to the philosopher, it is iron and corn, which have civilized mankind and ruined the human race."

The division of labor created by iron and corn led inevitably to the concept of property. The blacksmith needed the farmer's grain, and the farmer needed the blacksmith's tools; they began to exchange their products, and in doing so, they had to calculate the value of their labor and their land. This calculation led to the first claims of ownership: once a man had cultivated a piece of land, he felt he had a right to its harvest, and that right was soon extended to the land itself.

Property created a new kind of inequality: not the physical inequality of strength or age, which Rousseau calls "natural or physical inequality," but the social inequality of wealth, power, and prestige, which he calls "moral or political inequality."

This social inequality produced a state of war, but unlike Hobbes, Rousseau places this war at the *end* of the historical development, not at the beginning. It was not the natural man who fought for survival; it was the civilized man, corrupted by property and vanity (*amour-propre*), who fought for dominance. The rich, having accumulated land and goods, found themselves in a position of constant danger: they had no legal title to their wealth, which had been taken by force, and they were surrounded by a majority of poor people who had nothing to lose by taking it back.
## The Usurpation of the Social Contract
The solution to this crisis was the invention of the social contract, which Rousseau describes as the most clever trick in human history:

> "The rich man, pressed by necessity, conceived at last the most exquisite project that ever entered the human mind: to employ in his favor the very forces of those who attacked him, to make allies of his adversaries, and to give them institutions that would protect his property."

The rich man addressed the poor, proposing that they should join together to establish a power that would protect everyone from violence, maintain justice, and secure each person in his possessions. The poor, simple and tired of conflict, accepted the proposal: "They ran headlong into their chains, believing they were securing their liberty."

This contract was a fraud. It took a state of violent usurpation and turned it into a legal right. It secured the wealth of the rich and the poverty of the poor, establishing the state as an instrument for the protection of property rather than the preservation of liberty. The laws of civil society, Rousseau suggests, are merely the chains that keep the poor in place while the rich enjoy the harvest.
## The Psychology of the Modern Slave
The final section of the *Discourse* is a psychological study of the civilized man, whom Rousseau compares to a slave who has learned to love his chains.
He contrasts the natural man, who lives within himself, with the citizen, who lives entirely in the opinions of others:

> "The savage lives within himself; the sociable man, always outside himself, knows how to live only in the opinion of others, and it is, so to speak, from their judgment alone that he draws the experience of his own existence."

This "sociable man" is a figure of constant anxiety. He must perform a role, maintain a reputation, accumulate luxuries he does not need, and flatter those he despises, simply to feel that he exists. He has traded his physical health and his freedom for the "chimera" of social status.

This psychological analysis was highly influential. It prefigured the Marxist concept of alienation, the sociological study of consumer culture, and the Romantic rebellion against the conventions of the court and the salon. Rousseau's critique of civilization is not merely an economic or political argument; it is a diagnosis of a mental illness that has infected the modern world, making us strangers to our own feelings.
## The Rhetorical Strategy of the Treatise

Formally, the *Discourse on Inequality* is structured as a speculative history. Rousseau admits that we cannot know the state of nature in any scientific sense; it is a state that "no longer exists, which perhaps never existed, and probably never will exist, but of which it is nevertheless necessary to have correct notions."

He uses a variety of rhetorical strategies to make this speculative history persuasive. He uses dramatic set-pieces (the act of enclosure, the speech of the rich man); he draws analogies from the natural world and the travel literature of his day; and he writes in a style that is urgent, passionate, and directly addresses the reader's moral conscience.

This emotional intensity is what distinguishes Rousseau from his Enlightenment contemporaries. Where Voltaire and Montesquieu wrote with the cool irony of the salon, Rousseau wrote with the fury of the outsider. He does not seek to reform the institutions of his day; he seeks to expose their fundamental illegitimacy. The *Discourse* is not an administrative proposal; it is a declaration of war against the social order.
## The Open Wound

The essay ends with a vision of the contemporary world, in which the inequality of wealth and power has reached its extreme: a world where a child commands an old man, a fool leads wise men, and a handful of rich people are bloated with superfluities while the starving multitude lacks the necessities of life.
Rousseau concludes that this state of affairs is not only a moral failure, but a violation of natural law:

> "It is manifestly contrary to the law of nature, however defined, that a child should command an old man, that an imbecile should lead a wise man, and that a handful of people should gorge themselves with superfluities, while the starving multitude lacks common necessities."

This final sentence leaves the wound open. Rousseau does not offer a solution in the *Discourse*; he does not tell us how to return to the state of nature (which he admits is impossible) or how to build a just state (which he would attempt later in *The Social Contract*). He simply presents the diagnosis, leaving the reader with the realization that the civilization they inhabit is built on a fraud. The first man who enclosed a piece of land is still there, and the chains he forged are still around our necks.
Benjamin Franklin

**Original title:** *Father Abraham's Speech*, published as the preface to *Poor Richard's Almanack* (1758)  
**Date:** 1758 CE  
**Original language:** English  
**Country/tradition:** United States (Colonial America)  
**Period/movement:** The Enlightenment; American pragmatism; early capitalism  
**Genre:** Periodical essay; advice literature; compilation of maxims

"I stopped my horse lately where a great number of people were collected at a vendue of merchant goods. The hour of sale not being come, they were conversing on the badness of the times, and one of the company called to a plain clean old man, with white locks, 'Father Abraham, what think you of the times? Won't these heavy taxes quite ruin the country? How shall we ever be able to pay them? What would you advise us to?'" With this framing scene, Benjamin Franklin begins "The Way to Wealth," the preface to the twenty-fifth and final edition of his *Poor Richard's Almanack* in 1758. The setting is a "vendue", a public auction, where a crowd of colonials has gathered to buy imported luxuries, while complaining about the taxes imposed by the British crown and the general difficulty of making a living.

This framing scene is the pressure point of the essay. Franklin is writing at the transition from colonial dependency to independent commercial power. "The Way to Wealth" does not address the question of taxes or political representation through constitutional theory or legal arguments. It addresses it through the character of Father Abraham, who responds to the crowd by quoting the proverbs about industry, frugality, and self-reliance that had appeared in the *Almanack* over the past quarter-century. By compiling these maxims into a single speech, Franklin does not simply write a manual for financial success; he defines the moral and psychological basis of the American middle-class character, showing that true independence is not won on the battlefield or in the assembly, but in the ledger and the workshop.
## The Irony of the Auction
To read the essay well, you must watch the ending. After Father Abraham finishes his long sermon on thrift and industry, the auction begins:

> "The old gentleman ended his harangue, and the people heard it, and approved the doctrine, and immediately practiced the contrary, just as if it had been a common sermon; for the vendue began, and they began to buy extravagantly, notwithstanding all his cautions."

This double irony is the key to Franklin's humor. The crowd listens to the sermon, agrees with every word, praises the speaker's wisdom, and then immediately turns to buy the very luxury goods he had warned them against. They behave toward the economic sermon exactly as they behave toward Sunday sermons: they accept the theory and reject the practice.

Franklin's narrator, Poor Richard (Saunders), is the only one who actually changes his behavior: "I resolved to be the better for the echo of it; and though I had at first determined to buy stuff for a new coat, I went away resolved to wear my old one a little longer."

This resolution is a small, quiet act of independence. By refusing to buy the new coat, Richard escapes the debt, dependency, and vanity that the auction represents. The new coat is not just a piece of cloth; it is a "bondage" to the merchant and the tax-collector. The old coat is a symbol of self-determination.
## The Theology of the Ledger
The proverbs compiled in Father Abraham's speech are famous for their compression, rhythm, and home-spun wisdom:

> "God helps them that help themselves. Sloth, like rust, consumes faster than labor wears; while the used key is always bright. But dost thou love life, then do not squander time, for that's the stuff life is made of."

This view of time and labor was a secularization of the Puritan ethic that had shaped New England. For the seventeenth-century Puritans, industry and thrift were signs of religious election, duties performed for the glory of God. For Franklin, they are practical tools for the achievement of personal independence and civic virtue.

Franklin has no patience for the romantic view of poverty or the aristocratic contempt for work. He treats labor as a source of dignity and power: "He that hath a trade hath an estate, and he that hath a calling hath an office of profit and honor."

Frugality is the necessary companion to this industry. Franklin warns that a man who works hard but spends extravagantly is like a vessel with a leak: "A small leak will sink a great ship." He is particularly sharp on the purchase of imported luxuries, which he sees as a form of self-taxation that is far more expensive than any tax imposed by the government: "You call them goods, but if you do not take care, they will prove evils to some of you."

Debt is the ultimate consequence of this extravagance. Franklin describes the debtor as a slave who has surrendered his liberty to his creditor: "When you run in debt, you give to another power over your liberty. If you cannot pay at the time, you will be ashamed to see your creditor; you will be in fear when you speak to him; you will make poor pitiful sneaking excuses."

This psychological description of the debtor's shame is one of the most realistic passages in the essay. The loss of financial independence leads to a loss of moral character; the debtor is forced to lie, to flatter, and to hide, becoming a "sneaking" figure who has lost the right to speak truth in the public sphere.
## The Rise of the Bourgeois Character

"The Way to Wealth" was one of the most widely reprinted texts in the Atlantic world. It was translated into dozens of languages, published as a broadsheet to be hung on the walls of workshops, and distributed as a pamphlet for the education of the working class. It was the founding document of what the German sociologist Max Weber called the "Protestant Ethic and the Spirit of Capitalism."

Weber argued that Franklin's maxims represent the capitalist spirit in its purest form: the conviction that the accumulation of wealth is a moral duty, and that time, credit, and labor are commodities to be managed with rational calculation.

Yet Franklin's pragmatism is not simply about greed. He does not recommend wealth for its own sake, or for the luxury it can buy, luxury is, after all, the very thing he warns against. He recommends wealth because it is the only secure foundation for personal and political liberty. In a world where the poor are dependent on the rich, and the colonies are dependent on the mother country, the only way to be free is to be self-sufficient. Frugality is a political strategy: the man who does not need the merchant's goods cannot be controlled by the merchant's king.

This connection between private character and public politics was central to the American Revolution. The boycotts of British goods (the Non-Importation Agreements) that preceded the war were based on the principles of "The Way to Wealth": the colonists had to learn to wear homespun, drink domestic tea, and manage their own resources, before they could challenge the British army.
## The Prose of the Market

Formally, the essay is structured as a double frame. We have the narrator, Poor Richard, who introduces the speech; we have Father Abraham, who delivers the speech; and we have the proverbs themselves, which are quoted from the past editions of the *Almanack*. This structure allows Franklin to create a distance between himself and the moralizing voice of the sermon.

Poor Richard is a comic persona: he is poor, he is vanity-driven, and he is delighted to hear his own proverbs quoted by the wise old man: "The frequent mention of me by name by the old gentleman, did not a little please my vanity, though I was conscious that not a tenth part of the wisdom was my own."

This irony prevents the essay from becoming a dry, self-righteous lecture. Franklin is mocking his own ambition as a moral teacher, showing that the proverbs are common property, and that the teacher is subject to the same vanity and weakness as the crowd.

The style of the proverbs is characterized by its use of concrete, physical metaphors: keys, rust, ships, leaks, purses, coats. This is the language of the market and the workshop, designed to make the abstract virtues of industry and frugality look like material objects that can be handled and measured.
## The Open Ledger

The essay ends, as we saw, with the crowd buying extravagantly at the auction and Poor Richard walking away with his old coat. The sermon is over, the ledger remains open, and the conflict between our reason and our desires is unresolved.

"The Way to Wealth" remains a classic because it refuses to pretend that moral advice is easy to follow. Franklin knows that the crowd will always go to the auction, that vanity will always want the new coat, and that debt will always be a trap. The value of the essay is in its clear presentation of the choice: we can either practice the frugality that leads to independence, or run headlong into the dependency of the vendue. The plain old man with the white locks has spoken, the auctioneer has raised his hammer, and the crowd is already bidding.
Voltaire (François-Marie Arouet)

**Original title:** *Traité sur la tolérance*, specifically Chapter XXIII, "Prière à Dieu" (Prayer to God)  
**Date:** 1763 CE  
**Original language:** French  
**Country/tradition:** France  
**Period/movement:** The Enlightenment; anti-clerical campaigns  
**Genre:** Philosophical essay; political tract; philosophical prayer

"No longer then to men, but to thee, God of all beings, of all worlds, and of all ages, do I address myself: if it is permitted to feeble creatures, lost in the immensity of the universe, to dare to ask anything of thee..." With this invocation, Voltaire begins the twenty-third chapter of his *Treatise on Tolerance* (1763). This chapter, known as the "Prayer to God" (*Prière à Dieu*), is the emotional and rhetorical peak of the treatise, and has frequently been anthologized as a standalone essay "On Tolerance." The address is not a conventional prayer; it is a rhetorical performance that bypasses the ecclesiastical hierarchies and theological vocabularies of his day to appeal to a distant, benevolent creator on behalf of a suffering humanity.

This prayer is the pressure point of the essay. Voltaire is writing in the immediate aftermath of the judicial murder of Jean Calas, a Protestant merchant in Toulouse who had been falsely accused of murdering his son to prevent him from converting to Catholicism. Calas was tortured, broken on the wheel, and strangled by the authorities, in a trial that was driven by religious fanaticism and anti-protestant prejudice. Voltaire spent three years campaigning to clear Calas's name, writing letters, pamphlets, and this treatise to expose the cruelty of the Toulouse judges. By placing a prayer at the heart of his political campaign, Voltaire does not seek to defend the Protestant faith or to promote a new theology; he uses the language of religion to show that religious intolerance is not only a moral crime, but a ridiculous vanity when viewed from the scale of the universe.
## The Scale of the Universe and the Vanity of Dogma

The primary strategy of the "Prayer to God" is the reduction of human differences through the use of cosmic scale. Voltaire places the human spectator in the context of the new Copernican astronomy, looking at a vast, infinite universe in which the earth is merely a point:

> "Look down with pity on the errors which belong to our nature. Let not these errors prove our ruin. Thou hast not given us hearts to hate one another, nor hands to strangle one another; make us help one another to bear the burden of a painful and transitory life."

Against this immensity, the theological disputes that divide Christians, the differences in liturgy, the weight of vestments, the translation of scripture, look like the arguments of insects. Voltaire is particularly sharp on the pride of those who believe they have exclusive access to the divine will:

> "May the trifling differences between the clothes that cover our frail bodies, between our inadequate languages, our ridiculous customs, our imperfect laws, our foolish opinions, between all our conditions so disproportionate in our eyes and so equal in thine, may all these little variations which distinguish the atoms called 'men' not be the signals for hatred and persecution."

This description of human beings as "atoms" is a key Enlightenment move. By reducing humanity to physical particles, Voltaire strips away the claims of status, rank, and theological authority. The king's robes and the peasant's rags, the Catholic's Latin and the Protestant's vernacular, are merely "trifling differences" in the eyes of the creator. To kill a man because of these variations is as absurd as one grain of sand persecuting another because of its shade of color.

This deistic view of God is central to Voltaire's campaign. The God of the "Prayer" is not the active, jealous deity of the Old Testament or the dogmatic judge of the Counter-Reformation. He is the architect of a rational universe, who has given men reason to govern their conduct and pity to temper their passions. The responsibility for justice and tolerance lies with us, not with a divine intervention: "Thou hast not given us hearts to hate one another, nor hands to strangle one another."
## The Calas Affair and the Historical Context

To understand the fury behind the prayer, one must look at the details of the Calas trial, which Voltaire analyzes in the earlier chapters of the *Treatise*. The prosecution had relied on the testimony of superstitious neighbors, the rumors of the mob, and a medieval legal system that allowed torture to be used to extract confessions. Calas's execution was not an isolated event; it belonged to a history of religious violence in France that included the St. Bartholomew's Day Massacre (1572) and the Revocation of the Edict of Nantes (1685), which had forced hundreds of thousands of French Protestants into exile.

Voltaire's treatise is a systematic demolition of the arguments used to justify this persecution. He shows that the classical world, the Greeks and the Romans, was generally tolerant of religious differences, provided they did not threaten the stability of the state. He argues that the early Christians were persecuted not because of their beliefs, but because they refused to participate in the civic rituals of the empire. The introduction of systematic intolerance was, in his view, the work of the medieval church, which used the threat of heresy to maintain its wealth and political power.

The "Prayer to God" is the rhetorical resolution of this historical analysis. By turning from the details of legal corruption to a direct address to the creator, Voltaire forces his readers to look at the Calas trial from the perspective of eternity. The judges of Toulouse are no longer merely corrupt administrators; they are violators of the natural law of the universe.
## The Irony of the Deist

Formally, the "Prayer" is a model of Voltaire's ironic style, which is often called *persiflage*, a mixture of politeness, wit, and moral outrage. He adopts the form of the liturgy, using the pronouns of address (*Tu* or *Thou*) and the parallel structures of the psalms, but fills them with deistic and anti-clerical content.

The prayer is structured as a series of petitions: "May all men remember...", "May they look with horror...", "May the trifling differences...". The language is elevated, but the metaphors are drawn from the material world: atoms, clothes, coins, burdens. This mixture of the high-religious and the low-material is designed to expose the absurdity of religious pride:

> "May those who light candles at noon to worship thee bear with those who are content with the light of thy sun; may those who cover their robes with black wool to say that we must love thee not despise those who say the same thing in white linen."

The contrast between the "candles at noon" and the "light of thy sun" is a classic Voltairean image. The candle is the symbol of human artifice, theological dogma, and institutional religion; the sun is the symbol of natural reason, the deistic creator, and the common ground of humanity. To persecute someone because they prefer the sun to the candle is the ultimate form of intellectual blindness.

This irony is not merely a literary device; it is a political weapon. By making the persecutors look ridiculous, Voltaire strips them of their authority. The judge who breaks a man on the wheel because of his faith is no longer a figure of terror; he is an object of laughter, a foolish atom who has mistaken his own candle for the sun.
## The Legacy of the Treatise

Voltaire's campaign for Jean Calas was successful. In 1765, two years after the publication of the *Treatise*, the King's Council in Paris unanimously declared Calas innocent, cleared his family's name, and ordered the judges of Toulouse to pay damages. The trial became the first major victory for the new public opinion of the Enlightenment, demonstrating that the authority of the state and the church could be challenged by a writer with a printing press.

The *Treatise on Tolerance* became the foundational text of the modern secular movement, establishing the principle that the state has no right to police the conscience of its citizens. The "Prayer to God" remains the most famous section because it summarizes this principle in a form that is emotionally compelling: it translates the dry arguments of political philosophy into the language of the heart.
## The Silent Heavens
The essay ends with the prayer remaining in the air. The God of Voltaire does not speak; the heavens remain silent, and the "atoms" are left on their grain of sand to work out their own survival.

This silence is the final qualified conclusion. The prayer is not a petition for a miracle; it is a challenge to those who read it. If God will not intervene to stop the executioner, we must do so ourselves. The "light of the sun" is already there; the responsibility to see it belongs to us. The deist's prayer is, in the end, an invitation to action: it clears away the candles of dogma so that we can see one another's faces in the common light of day.
Oliver Goldsmith

**Original title:** "On National Prejudices", published in *The British Magazine* (August 1760); later anthologized in *Essays* (1765)  
**Date:** 1760 / 1765 CE  
**Original language:** English  
**Country/tradition:** Ireland / United Kingdom  
**Period/movement:** The Enlightenment; mid-eighteenth-century periodical essay  
**Genre:** Periodical essay; social satire; moral reflection

"As I am one of that sauntering tribe of mortals, who spend the greatest part of their time in taverns, coffee-houses, and other places of public resort, I have thereby an opportunity of observing an infinite variety of characters..." With this conversational opening, Oliver Goldsmith introduces his essay "On National Prejudices," published in *The British Magazine* in 1760. The setting is a London tavern, where the narrator, a self-described member of the "sauntering tribe," finds himself in the company of half a dozen gentlemen who are discussing the political situation of Europe. The conversation soon turns to national character, and one of the company, with a look of great solemnity, declares that the English are the only brave, generous, and free people on the earth, while the French are a nation of cowards, the Dutch are avaricious pack-horses, and the Germans are blockheads.

This tavern scene is the pressure point of the essay. Goldsmith is writing in 1760, during the Seven Years' War (1756–1763), but the surviving essay does not establish a direct connection to a particular campaign or press controversy. Its immediate subject is the psychology of national self-flattery. By examining the ease with which a speaker turns inherited national reputation into personal merit, Goldsmith argues that narrow patriotism can become a form of collective vanity, and proposes instead the ideal of the "citizen of the world" who treats other nations with greater fairness and curiosity.
## The Tavern Patriots and the Taxonomy of Prejudice

The core of the essay is the narrator's objection to the tavern patriot's declarations. When asked for his opinion, the narrator suggests that the other European nations also have their virtues: that the French are polite and lively, the Dutch are industrious and clean, and the Germans are patient and brave. This moderate response is met with silent disapproval by the company:

> "This declaration of mine was met with a general look of disgust by the whole company; one of them, with a sneer, told me he believed I had more of the French than the English in my blood; and another remarked that he was sorry to find a gentleman of my appearance so lacking in love for his country."

The psychology of this reaction is recorded with great accuracy. To the nationalist, any attempt to be fair to the enemy is treated as a form of treason; the world must be divided into absolute categories of good and evil, and the critic who refuses this division is accused of a lack of patriotism.

Goldsmith's narrator analyzes this prejudice not as an individual defect alone, but as a social habit. He argues that national prejudice is a lazy shortcut for the intellect: it allows a man to feel superior to others without the trouble of acquiring virtue or knowledge himself. The tavern patriot can feel himself the master of Europe simply by repeating the clichés of his class:

> "He who has no character of his own is always the readier to value himself upon the character of his country. He believes that he inherits the courage of his ancestors and the wealth of his merchants, without having contributed a single penny or a single act of bravery to either."

This critique of inherited merit places the essay in an Enlightenment register, but its force comes from the particular satire rather than from a general theory of the period. Goldsmith is arguing that virtue is an individual achievement, not a collective property. The citizen who boasts of his nation's greatness while living an idle, useless life is like a beggar who boasts of his father's estate.
## The "Citizen of the World" and the Cosmopolitan Ideal
Against the narrow patriotism of the tavern, Goldsmith proposes the ideal of the cosmopolitan:

> "Is it not much more generous, and more consistent with the character of a rational being, to look upon ourselves as citizens of the world? to consider the whole human race as one great family, and the different nations as different rooms in the same house?"

This image of the world as a "house" with different rooms is one of the most beautiful metaphors in eighteenth-century literature. It suggests that national differences are domestic variations rather than natural divisions. The French, the Dutch, and the Germans are not our enemies; they are our housemates, whose rooms have been decorated in different styles due to the accidents of history and climate.

The essay's cosmopolitan vocabulary belongs to a wider eighteenth-century debate about national character and human fellowship. This chapter does not treat that debate as a uniform Enlightenment consensus, or claim that Goldsmith speaks for every writer associated with a republic of letters. Its narrower point is that Goldsmith turns an abstract ideal into a test of everyday conversation: can a person admire a country without converting that admiration into contempt for everyone else?

Goldsmith's essay is an attempt to translate this intellectual cosmopolitanism into a daily practice of civil life. The "citizen of the world" is not a philosopher who refuses all local attachments; he is a gentleman who remains open to the variety of human life, who enjoys the company of foreigners, and who refuses to let the accidents of birth limit his sympathy.
## The Critique of Patriotism
Goldsmith is careful to distinguish between a rational love of one's country and the vulgar patriotism of the tavern:

> "I would not be understood to mean that we should have no affection for the country of our birth. A rational love of our country is a natural and necessary virtue; it is what leads us to obey the laws, to support the institutions, and to defend the state when it is genuinely threatened. But this love should be quiet, modest, and consistent with the respect we owe to the rest of mankind."

The target of the essay is the "vulgar" patriotism that is built on the hatred of others. Goldsmith presents this as a distortion of ordinary affection for home. The essay's own evidence is conversational and satirical, not a documented study of state propaganda, so its political implication should be stated carefully: language that turns national difference into contempt makes violence easier to imagine and defend.

Goldsmith's critique gains historical pressure from its 1760 setting, but the chapter does not infer a complete media history from the tavern scene. The essay gives us a small public exchange in which national stereotypes circulate as common sense. Its intervention is to interrupt that circulation, asking the reader to replace inherited assertion with observation, comparison, and self-scrutiny.
## The Conversational Grace of the Essay

Formally, "On National Prejudices" can be read in relation to the familiar-essay tradition associated with Steele and Addison, without requiring a direct line of influence for every feature. Goldsmith's language is conversational and comparatively plain, and its ease is part of the satire's method.

Goldsmith writes in the voice of the "saunterer", the relaxed, observant traveler who has no urgent business and no factional loyalties. This persona is crucial to the essay's work. Because the narrator is not an administrator or a politician, he has no interest in defending the policies of the state or the prejudices of the mob. He is free to observe, to listen, and to comment with the quiet irony of the spectator.

The transitions are quick and natural, moving from the tavern conversation to a historical reflection on Rome and Greece, to a philosophical analysis of the passions, and back to the tavern. The metaphors are drawn from the domestic sphere, houses, rooms, clothes, families, making the cosmopolitan ideal look like a natural extension of family life.
## The essay's final turn

The essay does not end with a narrated departure from the tavern. It ends by giving preference to the older figure of the "citizen of the world" over narrower national appellations. That ending keeps the argument modest. Goldsmith does not offer a programme for abolishing local attachment; he asks the reader to refuse the claim that love of country requires contempt for other countries.

The form of the conclusion is therefore less theatrical than the scene that precedes it. The narrator's final movement is conceptual: he turns from the company’s confident taxonomy of nations to a principle of enlarged fellowship. The essay leaves the reader with a choice of judgement rather than a documented change in the tavern patriots themselves. Its lasting pressure lies in that shift from inherited identity to examined sympathy.

chapters.title: 24. J. Hector St. John de Crèvecoeur: "What Is an American?"

content.value: J. Hector St. John de Crèvecoeur (Michel-Guillaume Saint-Jean de Crèvecoeur)

**Original title:** *Letters from an American Farmer*, Letter III, "What Is an American?"  
**Date:** 1782 CE  
**Original language:** English (originally drafted in English, later translated and expanded in French by the author)  
**Country/tradition:** France / United States  
**Period/movement:** The Enlightenment; early American republic; agrarianism  
**Genre:** Epistolary essay; travel literature; social geography

"What then is the American, this new man? He is either an European, or the descendant of an European, hence that strange mixture of blood, which you will find in no other country. I could point out to you a family whose grandfather was an Englishman, whose wife was Dutch, whose son married a French woman, and whose present four sons have now four wives of different nations." With this question and genealogical observation, the narrator of *Letters from an American Farmer*, writing under the persona of "Farmer James," begins his famous inquiry in Letter III: "What Is an American?" The focus is the "strange mixture of blood" that was then forming on the eastern seaboard of North America. The narrator is not interested in the political theory of the British constitution or the theological heritage of the Puritans; he is interested in the biological and social geography of the New World.

This focus on the "new man" is the pressure point of the essay. Crèvecoeur is writing during the American Revolutionary War, and the book was published in London in 1782, before the conflict had formally ended. The biographical circumstances behind the narrator's displacement should not be treated as identical with Farmer James's story: this chapter does not assert a specific family division, a flight as a suspected loyalist, or a completed personal loss of the farm without a separate biographical witness. "What Is an American?" is instead read here as a constructed attempt to explain to a European audience what made the British colonies in North America different from the old societies of Europe. Its language helped furnish a later vocabulary of American exceptionalism, but calling it the first such myth would overstate the evidence.
## The Rebirth of the Poor

The core of Crèvecoeur's argument is that America is a site of physical and moral resurrection for the poor of Europe. He contrasts the condition of the European peasant, who has no land, no political rights, and no hope of advancement, with the condition of the American farmer:

> "In Europe they were as so many useless plants, wanting vegetative mould, and refreshing showers; they withered, and were mowed down by want, hunger, and war; but now, by the power of transplantation, like all other plants they have taken root and flourished! They receive ample dust, and have become men."

The analogy with botany is typical of Crèvecoeur. He treats human beings as plants whose character is determined entirely by the "soil" in which they are placed. The European soil, crowded with landlords, kings, and priests, has exhausted its nutrients; the peasant is mowed down like grass. The American soil, open, cheap, and free from feudal obligations, allows the immigrant to "transplant" himself, taking root and developing into a fully realized human being.

This resurrection is achieved through labor. In America, the immigrant works for himself, not for a landlord or a bishop. The laws are simple, taxes are low, and the fruit of his labor belongs to his family: "We have no princes, for whom we toil, starve, and bleed: we are the most perfect society now existing in the world. Here man is free; as he ought to be; nor is this pleasing equality so transitory as many others."

Within Letter III, this is presented as a distinctive form of equality. It is not the equality of the Spartan barracks or the Platonic republic; it is the idealised equality of the family farm, where the independent cultivator appears free from the obligations that governed the European peasant.
## The Melting Pot and the New Race
The second key concept in the essay is the "melting" of different European nationalities into a single American identity:

> "He is an American, who leaving behind him all his ancient prejudices and manners, receives new ones from the new mode of life he has embraced, the new government he obeys, and the new rank he holds. He becomes an American by being received in the broad lap of our great Alma Mater. Here individuals of all nations are melted into a new race of men, whose labours and posterity will one day cause great changes in the world."

This description of the "melting" of nationalities prefigured the concept of the melting pot, which would become the dominant metaphor for American immigration in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries. Crèvecoeur is arguing that the immigrant must leave behind his "ancient prejudices", the religious wars, national rivalries, and class divisions of Europe, to participate in the new society.

In the letter's rhetoric, this melting is a transformation rather than a simple loss of identity. The American becomes a "new man" through the new government, social rank, and mode of life that the narrator associates with the farm. The description is aspirational: it presents the cultivator as active, industrious, and future-oriented, while leaving the exclusions and coercions of the colonial world in view only unevenly.

However, Crèvecoeur's definition of this "new race" is narrow: it is explicitly European. The letter's treatment of Native peoples is shaped by colonial categories, while the enslaved African Americans largely disappear from its idealised account. The later letters make that omission harder to sustain as a complete description of American society.
## The Contradictions of the Paradise

To read "What Is an American?" well, it should be read alongside the later letters in the collection. While Letter III presents an idyllic picture of the Middle Colonies, Letter IX, set in Charles-Town, shifts to a stark critique of slavery.

In Charles-Town, Farmer James encounters a world of luxury and cruelty that he compares with the worst features of European hierarchy. The climax of the letter is the discovery of a cage in a forest, in which an enslaved man has been left to expire while birds of prey attack him.

This scene complicates the agrarian myth of Letter III. The "new man" of freedom and equality cannot stand as a complete description of a society that also permits the planter's violence. The "Alma Mater" does not receive everyone in her broad lap; the later letter exposes the exclusions that the earlier ideal leaves aside.

The final letter, Letter XII, records a frontier family living under the threat of Revolutionary War. Farmer James says that he must abandon his farm and proposes to transport his family to a Native village where they may find safety. The text describes anticipated ruin and displacement, not a completed burning of the farm or a completed scattering of the family. The "new man" is therefore placed under the pressure of the violence that the earlier letter appears to have left behind in Europe. The ending is elegiac because the agrarian ideal has become precarious rather than secure.
## The Epistolary Style of the Farmer

Formally, the essay is structured as an epistolary travelogue, addressed to a fictional English gentleman named "Mr. F.B." This format allows Crèvecoeur to write in a voice that is personal, conversational, and direct, using the persona of the simple farmer to disarm the reader's skepticism.

The language is rich in sensory detail: the smell of the soil, the sight of the clearing, the sounds of the birds, the progress of the crops. This material realism is the signature of Crèvecoeur's style. He does not write about America as an abstract concept; he writes about it as a physical place, a landscape that is being transformed by human labor:

> "I go to my daily work with a mind that is quiet and satisfied. I look at my wife, who is busy in the dairy; I look at my children, who are playing in the yard; I look at my crops, which are growing in the field. This is my kingdom; this is my empire."

Later readers have placed this domestic focus within an American pastoral tradition that can be read alongside writers such as Thomas Jefferson, Henry David Thoreau, and Wendell Berry. A direct line of influence need not be claimed. The passage matters because it links the health of the family, the imagined health of the community, and the cultivation of the land.
## The Vanishing Frontier

Letter III ends within the narrator's idealised account of the farm; the collection's final letter later turns to war, fear, and contemplated departure. The picture is therefore never as complete as the rhetoric of the "new man" suggests.

"What Is an American?" remains a powerful account of American identity because it captures both the promise and the limits of the project. It describes a society imagined as new, free, and egalitarian, while the collection's later letters expose the violence and exclusion that the ideal cannot absorb. Farmer James's definition is persuasive precisely because the rest of the book makes its conditions and omissions visible.

chapters.title: 25. Mary Wollstonecraft: "On the Pernicious Effects Which Arise from the Unnatural Distinctions Established in Society"

content.value: Mary Wollstonecraft

**Original title:** *A Vindication of the Rights of Woman*, Chapter IX, "Of the Pernicious Effects Which Arise from the Unnatural Distinctions Established in Society"  
**Date:** 1792 CE  
**Original language:** English  
**Country/tradition:** England  
**Period/movement:** The Enlightenment; early feminism; radical political philosophy  
**Genre:** Philosophical essay; political treatise; feminist critique

"From the respect paid to property flow, as from a poisoned fountain, most of the evils and vices which render this world such a dreary scene to the contemplative mind." With this opening metaphor, Mary Wollstonecraft begins the ninth chapter of *A Vindication of the Rights of Woman* (1792). The image of the "poisoned fountain" is both a moral and a political statement. It locates the source of human vice not in natural depravity or divine decree, but in a specific social arrangement: the worship of wealth and the "unnatural distinctions" of rank, property, and gender that it supports.

This opening assertion is the pressure point of the chapter. The larger *Vindication* participates in the rights debates of the revolutionary era, but Chapter IX makes its case through a more focused movement from property and rank to domestic dependence and civil standing. Wollstonecraft argues that unequal social arrangements deform the character of both the privileged and the dependent. Her claim that moral reform requires greater equality is presented through polemic, imagined examples, and appeals to duty rather than through a neutral survey of society.
## The Corruption of the Rich and the Idle
One prominent target is the idle woman of fashion, whom Wollstonecraft presents as a product as well as a reproducer of the distinctions she criticizes:

> "A girl is habituated to luxury and show, and taught to look upon these things as her only security. She marries for a settlement, and then spends her life in the pursuit of trivial pleasures, neglecting her children and corrupting her household."

This description of the fashionable woman is both moral polemic and social analysis. Wollstonecraft represents women whose education, livelihood, and civil standing are constrained by rank, wealth, and expectations of beauty. In her account, dependence encourages a life organized around pleasing appearances and domestic status, leaving women without the independent exercise of reason and useful activity that she regards as necessary to virtue.

In Wollstonecraft's polemical account, idleness and inherited status deform relations across the household and the wider society. She links the pressure to appear pleasing with vanity, dependence, and the weakening of domestic duties. The language of slavery is an analogy within her argument about social dependence, not a claim that the situations she describes are identical in every respect to chattel slavery.

Wollstonecraft's critique extends to the men of the same class. The nobleman or the rich heir, who inherits his position and wealth without the need for labor, is corrupted by his own privilege: "The respect paid to property... makes him believe that he is a superior being, and he is soon incapacitated for the duties of a man and a citizen."
## The Poisoned Fountain of Property Worship

Underneath the domestic critique is an analysis of how property and wealth organize esteem. Wollstonecraft argues that their influence can displace natural affection and the duties through which she believes character is formed:

> "The respect paid to property... is the great obstacle to the progress of virtue. It makes us value a man for what he has, rather than for what he is, and turns the domestic life into a scene of financial calculation."

The chapter does not offer a systematic history of marriage markets. Its sharper claim is that when wealth, rank, and beauty determine esteem, domestic affection is subordinated to social calculation. Wollstonecraft contrasts that condition with a household in which husband and wife are sufficiently independent to perform their duties and exercise sympathy.

The chapter therefore treats the household as one place where social values become habits. Its contrast is between relationships governed by rank and relationships supported by mutual duty, useful work, affection, and enough material security to make generosity possible. This is a normative model advanced by Wollstonecraft, not an empirical description of every family.

Against this corruption, Wollstonecraft proposes a morality based on exertion, independence, and useful duties. She argues that women must be independent of men if they are to be virtuous and useful, and she imagines a society in which both sexes have civil responsibilities rather than merely inherited status.
## The Call for Economic and Political Independence

The most radical section of the essay is Wollstonecraft's call for the professional and political emancipation of women. She argues that women should be allowed to study medicine, run businesses, and participate in politics:
> "I may excite laughter, by hinting that women ought to have representatives, instead of being arbitrarily governed by men without having any direct share in the deliberations of government."

The reference to "exciting laughter" registers Wollstonecraft's awareness that female representation could be received as an incongruous proposal. She nevertheless connects civil standing with moral duty: if women are rational beings and citizens, their independence and participation cannot be separated from the responsibilities society assigns to them.

She is particularly sharp on the limited employment open to educated women. She names medicine, farming, shopkeeping, and the work of education as possible forms of useful activity, while noting the humiliations attached to governessing and other positions treated as menial. The point is not a modern catalogue of professions but an argument that women need a recognized civil existence, whether married or single.
## The Prose of Revolutionary Argument

Formally, the chapter is structured as a philosophical treatise, but its reasoning repeatedly becomes scene, satire, apostrophe, and imagined social arrangement. The larger *Vindication* engages debates associated with writers such as Locke, Rousseau, and Paine; within this chapter, Rousseau is explicitly invoked as a theorist of sexual distinction, while Wollstonecraft turns the language of reason, duty, and rights toward female independence.

The style is characterized by its emotional intensity and its urgent, direct address. Wollstonecraft does not write with the cool irony of Voltaire or the balanced structure of Johnson; she writes with the passion of a reformer who is participating in a historical crisis. The sentences are long, energetic, and full of moral indignation:

> "It is time to effect a revolution in female manners, time to restore to them their lost dignity, and to make them, as a part of the human species, labor to reform themselves, that they may reform the world."

The chapter's reformist rhetoric connects domestic conduct to civil order. Rather than supplying a detailed account of French constitutional developments, it argues that professions of liberty and equality lose force when women remain dependent, uneducated, and without an independent civil existence.
## The Unresolved Revolution

The chapter ends not with a report on French legislators but with an appeal to men to assist in emancipating women into rational fellowship. Wollstonecraft imagines that men would gain more observant daughters, affectionate sisters, faithful wives, reasonable mothers, and better citizens if women were no longer required to practise slavish obedience.

The appeal is deliberately reciprocal rather than narrowly legislative. Wollstonecraft links women's emancipation to men's willingness to exchange mastery for rational fellowship, while retaining her own period's language of marriage, motherhood, and domestic duty. The chapter therefore contains both a powerful demand for civil independence and a historically situated account of the roles through which she imagines that independence being exercised.

This chapter remains central to the political argument of the *Vindication* because it shows how private relations and public arrangements are inseparable in Wollstonecraft's reasoning. The household becomes a testing ground for her larger principle: rights, duties, education, and independence must be distributed in ways that allow moral agency to develop. The poisoned fountain is therefore not merely an image of individual vice; it is her figure for a social order in which property and rank distort the conditions of virtue.
Washington Irving

**Original title:** *The Sketch Book of Geoffrey Crayon, Gent.*, "The Mutability of Literature: A Colloquy in Westminster Abbey"  
**Date:** 1819 CE  
**Original language:** English  
**Country/tradition:** United States  
**Period/movement:** Romanticism; early American literature  
**Genre:** Personal essay; dream vision; literary colloquy

In the quiet, dust-laden atmosphere of the library of Westminster Abbey, Geoffrey Crayon, the wandering American narrator of Washington Irving’s *Sketch Book* (1819), finds himself holding an ancient, leather-bound volume. It is a little thick quarto, printed in black-letter, whose pages have turned brown with age. As he turns the leaves, a voice speaks from the paper: the book itself, having been shut up for more than two centuries in this quiet room, begins to complain about its fate, lamenting the dust, the confinement, and the steady erosion of its language.

This talking book is the pressure point of "The Mutability of Literature." Irving is writing at the beginning of the nineteenth century, an American visitor in the heart of the British Empire, exploring the monuments of a history that his own country had recently broken from. The essay does not look to the political future or the commercial expansion of the United States. It looks to the decay of language itself. By having the ancient quarto argue with Crayon about the vanity of authorship, Irving investigates the transience of literary fame, showing that the very medium through which we seek immortality, language, is a shifting sand that dissolves our words almost as soon as they are written.
## The Dialogue with the Quarto

The core of the essay is the conversation between Crayon and the little book. The quarto is indignant about its neglect: it believes that because it was written by a man of learning, printed with care, and placed in a royal library, it should be read by every generation. Crayon, however, is forced to explain the harsh reality of literary history:

> "The quarto was astonished to find that it was no longer read. It believed that its language, which was the English of Queen Elizabeth's court, was the absolute standard of beauty and truth, and could not understand how it had become obsolete. I had to explain that our language is like our fashions: it changes with every age, and the writer who writes for the present will soon find himself a stranger to the future."

Crayon's analysis is historicist and skeptical. He argues that language changes across generations, carrying literary reputations with it. Chaucer's language requires mediation for many modern readers; the quarto's older English has already become difficult; and Crayon's own language will likewise be subject to alteration.

This linguistic mutability destroys the author's search for immortality. The writer who spends his life polishing his style in the hope of outlasting the pyramids is building on a foundation of fog. His words will lose their meaning, his metaphors will become obscure, and his book will be left on the shelf, a monument to a language that no one speaks.
## The Exception of Shakespeare

Against this general law of decay, the quarto objects by pointing to William Shakespeare. If literature is mutable, why has Shakespeare retained an unusually durable place in English literary culture?
Crayon's response is one of the most famous passages in early American criticism:

> "Shakespeare is the exception that proves the rule. He did not write in the cold, artificial style of the schools; he wrote in the language of the heart. His characters are not the types of a fashion or a class; they are the representatives of our common nature. Because he was true to nature, nature has remained true to him."

Shakespeare's language, Crayon suggests, is durable because it is rooted in recognisable human experience rather than in a style that belongs only to one moment. The claim is Irving's literary argument, not a neutral account of Shakespeare's diction or of his learned contemporaries.

This explanation belongs to a Romantic-era tendency to value Shakespeare's relation to human nature over strict classical correctness. Irving participates in that conversation and uses it to frame a moral: writing may outlast a particular fashion when its language continues to make experience legible. The claim remains a critical proposition, not a guarantee of literary permanence.
## The American in the Abbey

The setting of the essay is crucial to its tone. Irving places Crayon among the cloisters, monuments, and library of Westminster Abbey, where the material remains of older literary culture surround a modern act of reading. For an American visitor, the scene creates a distance between inherited English memory and the narrator's mobile, self-conscious perspective, but the essay presents that distance as a mood and literary device rather than a complete political history.

Crayon is drawn to the Abbey's architecture and historical associations, yet he also notices the silence and neglect surrounding the books. The dialogue with the quarto turns that physical setting into a meditation on preservation: a book may survive materially while its language and reputation become difficult to recover.

The dialogue with the quarto is a version of this cultural encounter. Crayon, the representative of the new, mobile world, is looking at the quarto, the representative of the old, static world. His tone is not triumphant; it is elegiac. He does not celebrate the fact that the old books are neglected; he regrets it, recognizing that his own books will one day suffer the same fate:

> "I looked around the library with a feeling of melancholy. Here were thousands of books, each representing the labor of a life, each containing the hopes of an author for immortality, and almost all of them were silent. They were like the tombs in the cloisters: monuments to a name that has been forgotten."

This melancholy is characteristic of the episode's rhetoric. The traveller's meditation on the Abbey becomes a reflection on the temporary nature of reputation, without requiring every monument or volume to stand as documentary evidence of cultural decline.
## The Style of the Sketch

Formally, "The Mutability of Literature" is a sketch-like colloquy. It combines a situated walk, a dreamlike interruption, and a conversation that allows literary history to become a dramatic exchange. The form is visual and episodic, but its atmosphere is also an instrument of argument.

The language is characterized by its liquid, flowing quality, its use of soft adjectives and quiet transitions. Irving does not argue; he describes. He guides the reader through the library, showing the dust on the shelves, the light through the gothic windows, and the physical details of the quarto, before initiating the dialogue. The fantasy of the talking book is presented not as a supernatural event, but as a natural consequence of the place: the room is so quiet, so old, and so full of the past that it seems natural for the books to speak.

The visual focus shows how a place can become an argument about reading and memory. A direct line from this piece to the later work of Hawthorne, Henry James, or Robert Louis Stevenson is not established here; the comparison belongs to literary interpretation rather than verified influence. The value of the sketch comes from its capacity to capture the texture of a place, transforming a physical landscape into a state of mind.
## The Closing of the Quarto

The essay ends when the verger arrives to close the library. The quarto falls silent and its clasps are closed. Crayon later returns to the library two or three times and cannot discover whether the colloquy took place or was another of his day-dreams.

This ending preserves the uncertainty at the centre of the piece. The conversation has altered the reader's sense of the books, but it does not settle whether the book literally spoke. Irving leaves literary mutability between material evidence and imaginative experience: the volume remains, while the status of the encounter cannot be fixed.

chapters.title: 27. Leigh Hunt: "Getting Up on Cold Mornings"

content.value: Leigh Hunt

**Original title:** "Getting Up on Cold Mornings", published in *The Indicator* (January 19, 1820)  
**Date:** 1820 CE  
**Original language:** English  
**Country/tradition:** England  
**Period/movement:** Romanticism; Cockney School  
**Genre:** Personal essay; familiar essay; humorous sketch

"An Italian author, Giulio Cordara, a Jesuit, wrote a poem upon insects, which he begins by declaring that those little creatures were created for the purpose of chastising the pride of man, by showing him that there are beings more active, more industrious, and more numerous than himself. I have always thought of this poem when I have been asked to get up on a cold morning." With this reference to a forgotten Italian Jesuit and his insects, Leigh Hunt begins "Getting Up on Cold Mornings," published in his weekly sheet *The Indicator* in 1820. The connection is comic and oblique: the insect's industry is a reproach to human laziness, and the act of getting out of bed on a freezing winter morning is the ultimate test of this industry.

This delay in bed is the pressure point of the essay. Hunt turns an ordinary act of resistance to cold into a comic argument about the claims of duty, health, and industry.
