"Getting Up on Cold Mornings" can be read as a humorous challenge to the assumption that usefulness and early rising settle the value of an experience. The essay does not mount a systematic social theory; it stages a debate between the warm body under the blankets and the cold room outside.
## The Dialogue of the Blankets

The core of the essay is the internal debate between the narrator's body and his conscience. Conscience, representing the voice of duty, tells him that he must get up: that he has work to do, that he is wasting time, and that early rising is good for the health. The body, representing the voice of the blankets, responds with a series of brilliant, mock-logical objections:

> "The argument for getting up is that it is healthy and industrious. But what is health? It is the balance of the animal spirits. And how can the spirits be balanced when the body is shocked by a sudden transition from warmth to freezing cold? To get up is to commit a violence against nature."

The narrator is particularly sharp on the figures of the "early risers" who are held up as examples for the young. He notes that the people who get up early are often bad-tempered, pedantic, and boring: they spend their mornings boasting of their early rising rather than doing anything useful: "They are like the man who got up at four in the morning to tell his neighbors that he was awake."

This parody of moral duty is a key Hunt strategy. By treating the voice of conscience as a pedantic bore and the body's laziness as a rational philosophy, he strips the work ethic of its moral authority. The warm bed is not a site of sin; it is a site of sanity, a refuge where a man can find a quiet perspective on the busy, anxious world outside.
## The Sensory Reality of the Cold
Part of what makes the essay convincing is the precision of its sensory detail. Hunt describes the physical sensations of the winter morning with clinical accuracy:

> "The window is covered with frost; the water in the pitcher is frozen; the air is like a knife. You put out a hand to test the air, and immediately pull it back under the blankets. The bed is a small kingdom of warmth, and the room is a wilderness of cold."

This contrast between the "kingdom" and the "wilderness" is the spatial axis of the essay. The bed is a civilized space, comfortable, secure, and self-contained; the room is a hostile environment that must be negotiated with caution.

The narrator's account of the servant who comes to light the fire is a masterpiece of comic observation. The servant is a figure of quiet malice: he arrives with a face red from the cold, reports that the water is frozen, and then stands by the bed waiting for the master to get up. His presence is a physical reproach: he has been up for hours, he has lit the fire, and now he wants the master to suffer the same cold that he has survived.

Hunt's narrator does not yield to this pressure. He negotiates, he delays, he asks for more coal, he complains about the draft, using every rhetorical tool at his disposal to prolong his stay under the blankets. This delay is not merely laziness; it is a performance, an attempt to extract the maximum pleasure from the threshold between sleep and waking.
## The Cockney School and the Pleasures of the Everyday

The essay's place in Hunt's literary circle can be read alongside the hostile "Cockney School" label. In 1817, *Blackwood's Magazine* used that phrase for Hunt and associated writers including John Keats and William Hazlitt. The label was polemical rather than a neutral name for a self-declared school, and this chapter does not treat it as proof that every writer in the group shared one programme.

The hostile reviews attacked the writers' diction, learning, social position, and political associations. Those attacks help explain why ordinary pleasures could become a literary and cultural issue, but they do not establish that the critics formed a single consistent case against every text associated with Hunt.

"Getting Up on Cold Mornings" can be read in relation to that controversy without being treated as a direct reply to a particular review. Hunt does not apologise for his interest in the trivial; he makes the small, daily struggle against cold a subject worthy of literary art. The familiar essay becomes a form in which wit and learning can be applied to an experience usually dismissed as too ordinary for serious attention.

The essay's title also invites a broader reading of what an indicator might do: direct attention to small pleasures that are overlooked in the rush of business. The warm bed and the quiet morning are not treated merely as distractions from the good life; the essay asks what kind of value can be found in them.
## The Conversational Style of the Indicator

Formally, the essay is written in a style that is loose, conversational, and direct. Hunt writes as if he were speaking to a friend over breakfast, using short sentences, exclamation marks, and rhetorical questions to maintain the illusion of immediacy.

He uses classical and historical references not to show off his learning, but to make the trivial look grand. The Jesuit Cordara and his insects, the Emperor Augustus and his morning habits, the rules of the scholastic philosophers, these are all brought down to the level of the blankets, used to justify the narrator's refusal to get out of bed.

The style shows how the familiar essay can make a small bodily experience carry argumentative pressure. It does not need to be treated as the established source of the nineteenth-century personal column, or as a direct influence on Thackeray, Stevenson, or Chesterton. Its value lies in the way it plays with ideas, mocks conventions, and makes the small-scale available for serious attention.
## The Wet Sole

The essay concludes with the narrator's eventual defeat. The servant has brought the hot water, the fire has caught, and the excuses have been exhausted. The narrator is forced to put his foot out of bed and touch the cold floor:
> "The moment arrives; the blankets are thrown off; you make a leap for the clothes. The sole of the foot touches the floor, it is wet. The servant has spilled the water. The drama is over."

This final detail of the "wet sole" is the comic resolution. The philosophy of the blankets collapses before the reality of the spilled water. The narrator is out of bed, the cold room has won, and the day has begun.

Hunt leaves the reader with a double impression. We laugh at the narrator's excuses and his physical terror of the cold, but we also remember the warmth of the bed and the justice of his rebellion. The work ethic has won the battle, but the blankets have won the argument. The wet sole is the print of our return to the ground, but the memory of the warmth remains as a promise of another morning.
Charles Lamb

**Original title:** *The London Magazine* (January 1821), later collected in *Essays of Elia* (1823)  
**Date:** 1821 CE  
**Original language:** English  
**Country/tradition:** England  
**Period/movement:** Romanticism; Cockney School  
**Genre:** Personal essay; familiar essay; melancholic reflection

"Every man hath two birthdays: two days, at least, in every year, which set him upon revolving the lapse of time, as it affects his mortal duration. The one is that which in an especial manner he calleth his. The other is the New Year." With this parallel opening, Charles Lamb, writing under the persona of Elia, begins "New Year's Eve," one of the most searching and melancholic essays in his 1821 collection. The tone is immediately reflective: the ringing of the bells at midnight is not a signal for celebration, but a knell that reminds the listener of his own mortality.

This auditory reminder is the pressure point of the essay. Lamb is writing in his late forties, clerk at the East India House, survivor of a family tragedy, his sister Mary had killed their mother in a fit of temporary insanity, and Charles had taken responsibility for her care, sacrificing his own hopes of marriage and family. "New Year's Eve" is his final reckoning with the passage of time and the reality of death. The essay rejects the consolations of philosophy and the conventional hopes of religion in favor of an honest, physical account of his fear of death and his love for the material world. By placing this confession in the mouth of Elia, Lamb models a new kind of personal essay: the intimate, self-critical, and unapologetically subjective exploration of the mind's dark corners.
## The Two Elias: The Child and the Clerk
The first movement of the essay is a division of the self. Elia distinguishes between the man he is now, the middle-aged clerk, tired, cynical, and marked by his errors, and the child he once was:

> "I can look upon the child Elia with a kind of pity and affection. He was a different being from myself: he had hopes that I have lost, a innocence that I have surrendered, and a capacity for joy that has been dried up by the years. I do not feel responsible for his errors; I look at him as if he were a stranger whom I loved."

This separation of the past self from the present self is a key Lamb strategy. By treating his childhood self as an object of study, he avoids both self-congratulation and self-pity. The child is a separate character, a "ghost" that visits the clerk's study to remind him of what he has lost.

This division of the self is also a critique of the idea of personal continuity. We do not remain the same person throughout our lives; we are a sequence of selves, each dying in turn to make room for the next. The New Year is the moment when this sequence becomes visible: we look back at the years and see a row of dead Elias, stretching back to the nursery.
## The Confession of the Coward

The middle section of the essay is a confession of his fear of death that was controversial in its day for its honesty. Elia admits that he has no desire to die, and that he hates the philosophical and religious arguments that try to reconcile him to his end:

> "I am not content to die. I have no speed to be a spirit. I want to remain a man, in this body, on this earth. I love the streets of London, the light of candles, the smell of old books, the taste of food, the faces of my friends. I do not want to be translated into a cold, abstract heaven where none of these things exist."

This rejection of the "spiritual" afterlife in favor of the "material" world is the emotional core of the essay. Elia is a deist of the senses: his heaven is not a temple of gold and lapis lazuli, but a room with a fire, a bottle of wine, a deck of cards, and a friend. He has no interest in the "immortality of the soul" if it means the loss of the physical details that constitute his identity:

> "Shall I go to a place where there is no book to read, no candle to light, no street to walk, no friend to talk to? Where I must sit in a white robe and sing forever? That is not a heaven; that is a prison of light."

This honesty is what distinguishes Lamb from his contemporaries. The Victorian writers who followed him would spend a great deal of time writing about the "beauty of death" and the "dignity of the grave." Lamb refuses this posture. He admits that death is a horror, a "snatcher" that takes away everything we care about, and that the only honest response to it is fear and resistance.
## The London of Elia

The material world that Elia loves is specifically the world of London. Throughout his essays, he returns to the streets of the city, Fleet Street, the Strand, the Temple, the Covent Garden market, as the primary sites of his imagination.

Unlike the Romantic poets (Wordsworth, Coleridge), who sought out the wilderness of the Lake District or the mountains of Wales to find the sublime, Lamb found his sublime in the crowd. The noise of the coaches, the light of the shops, the faces of the passengers, the very smell of the coal-smoke were all sources of energy for his mind:

> "I have no passion for groves and valleys. The room in which I write is my forest; the streets of London are my mountains. I find in the crowd of Fleet Street a more delightful variety than in all the lakes of Cumberland."

This urban pastoral was a key part of the Cockney School's aesthetic. It asserted that the city is not a site of pollution and corruption, but a rich, complex human landscape that is worthy of the same poetic attention that the Romantics reserved for nature. The "pleasures of the town" are the source of our finest moral feelings: it is in the crowd that we learn sympathy, curiosity, and the art of conversation.
## The Prose of the Parenthesis

Formally, "New Year's Eve" is a masterpiece of the familiar style, which Lamb developed through a combination of seventeenth-century vocabulary (Robert Burton, Thomas Browne) and modern, conversational syntax.

The prose is characterized by its use of parentheses, dashes, and digressions. Elia does not write in a straight line; his mind moves by association, memory, and qualification. He starts a sentence about the new year, stops to describe a book he bought, qualifies his description with a parenthetical note about the price, and then returns to the main thought.

This structure is the formal expression of his skepticism. He refuses the "Methods" and the "Systems" of the academy, because he believes they distort the complexity of actual experience. The mind does not think in systems; it thinks in fragments, memories, and sudden changes of feeling. The essay's job is to record these fragments with fidelity, allowing the reader to see the texture of a mind in real time.

The use of archaic words, "inditer," "phantasm," "gosling", is also a key feature of the style. These words are not used to show off his learning; they are used to create a distance between Elia and the contemporary world, giving the prose a quiet, slightly dusty quality that matches the atmosphere of his study.
## The Toast to the Future

The essay concludes with a turn to the immediate. The bells have stopped ringing, the old year is dead, and the new year has arrived. Elia does not make any resolutions or offer any optimistic predictions. He simply pours himself a glass of wine and proposes a toast:

> "We are still here, my friends. The snatcher has not taken us yet. The fire is still bright, the candle is still burning, and the wine is still in the cup. Let us drink to the present, and let the future take care of itself."

This toast is the final qualified conclusion. It is a rebellion against the passage of time: a decision to inhabit the immediate moment with as much pleasure and clarity as we can manage, in spite of the dark mist that hangs over the end of the bridge. Elia has spoken, the glass is raised, and the candle is still burning in the room.
Charles Lamb

**Original title:** "Dream-Children: A Reverie" (first published in *The London Magazine*, January 1822; later collected in *Essays of Elia*, 1823)  
**Date:** 1822 CE  
**Original language:** English  
**Country/tradition:** England  
**Period/movement:** Romanticism; Cockney School  
**Genre:** Personal essay; familiar essay; dream vision

"Children love to listen to stories about their elders, when they were children; to stretch their imagination to the conception of a traditionary great-uncle, or a grandame, whom they never saw." With this gentle observation, Charles Lamb, writing under the persona of Elia, begins "Dream-Children: A Reverie," published in *The London Magazine* in January 1822. The setting is the domestic hearth, where the bachelor Elia sits by the fire, telling his two children, Alice and John, stories about a great house that the essay places in Norfolk. Biographical accounts connect Lamb's grandmother Field with Blakesware in Hertfordshire, so the essay's geography should be treated as part of its imaginative Elia narration rather than silently harmonized with biography.

This fireside scene is the pressure point of the essay. The children are not merely an audience; they are active participants in the narrative, reacting with gestures, tears, and questions to the details of the past. Yet the title has already warned the reader that this domestic scene is a "reverie," a dream of what might have been. By allowing the dream-children to dissolve at the end of the narrative, Lamb joins the grief of recent bereavement to the fantasy of an absent family, making memory and desire formally inseparable.
## The Landscape of Memory: Blakesware and Grandmother Field

The first movement of the essay is a descent into the geography of childhood. Elia describes a great house in Norfolk, with its old ornaments, its carved story of the Children in the Wood, and its garden of peaches, nectarines, and other fruit. Biographical accounts identify Lamb's maternal grandmother, Elizabeth Field, with the housekeeper at Blakesware in Hertfordshire, but the essay itself gives Norfolk and turns the remembered house into an imaginative setting.
The center of this landscape is Great-Grandmother Field, whom Elia describes as pious, good, widely respected, and entrusted with the care of the house:

> "She was a woman of extraordinary piety and goodness, beloved by everyone who knew her. She lived in the great house as its keeper, maintaining its dignity even when the owner had abandoned it for a modern villa. She knew the history of every room, the name of every ancestor on the walls, and was the true spirit of the place."

Field can be read as a figure of continuity within the country house, but the essay also gives her a sharply personal presence. She had been, in her youth, an admired dancer, and in old age her body was bent by illness while her moral stature remained intact in Elia's memory. The passage is a recollection shaped by affection, not a complete social history of the country house.

Elia's memory of visits to the house is characterized by imaginative attention. He recalls the old rooms, the garden, the forbidden fruit, and the contrast between his own quiet habits and the more energetic boyhood of John L. The house becomes less a documented setting than a theatre in which remembered objects, family stories, and later grief can be made to coexist.

The effect is important for the essay's method. Lamb turns apparently minor objects and gestures into carriers of emotional history, allowing a remembered house to generate the essay's movement from anecdote to reverie. That is a formal reading of the passage, not a claim that Blakesware can be treated as a transparent record of the writer's childhood.
## The Figure of the Dead Brother
The narrative moves from the grandmother to the figure of the uncle, John L., who represents the physical energy and the tragic losses of the family:

> "John was a handsome, high-spirited boy, the favorite of his grandmother and the leader of all our childhood games. He was brave, generous, and full of life; but he died in his youth, and his death left a gap in our lives that could never be filled."

John L. is closely connected to Charles Lamb's real brother, John Lamb, whose death on 26 October 1821 is recorded in Lamb's correspondence and biography. The essay's initial presents the figure as part of the Elia fiction, while its account of childhood care, illness, and belated grief invites a biographical reading. No claim of a prolonged estrangement or of a single known compositional motive is necessary to establish that connection.

In the essay, Elia describes how death changes the scale of remembered attachment. John is recalled through his bravery, physical energy, earlier care for the lame-footed child, and the narrator's regret that he had not always made allowances for John's later pain. The brother becomes, in memory, both a vivid childhood presence and an object of belated self-reproach.

This elegiac tone is the emotional core of the essay. Publication followed John Lamb's death by only a few months, so the timing makes a biographical relation plausible, but the text remains a crafted Elia narrative rather than a diary entry. The dream-children provide an audience through which private sorrow can be staged as domestic conversation.
## The Dissolution of the Vision

The climax of the essay is the sudden transition from the dream to waking reality. As Elia describes his seven-year courtship of Alice W, n, the children's forms begin to grow faint. Biographical accounts have associated this figure with an earlier love, often named Ann Simmons, but the essay itself supplies only the fictionalized initial and the history of rejection:

> "While I was thus telling them the story of their mother's beauty, and how she had rejected me for another, I looked at the children, and their forms began to grow dim, and their eyes seemed to recede into the distance. They spoke to me with a voice that was like the rustling of leaves: 'We are not of Alice, nor of thee, nor are we children at all. The children of Alice call Bartrum father. We are nothing; less than nothing, and dreams. We are only what might have been.'"

The dream-children do not simply vanish; their speech makes their non-existence part of the narrative. They insist that they are not children of Alice and Elia, and that Alice's children call Bartrum father. The detail gives the fantasy an empirical surface while simultaneously exposing it as a construction of desire.
The transition back to reality is recorded with quiet, physical realism:
> "I awakened. I found myself in my bachelor armchair, where I had fallen asleep. The fire was nearly out; the room was dark; and Bridget was sitting by my side."

Bridget is the faithful companion beside the waking narrator. Biographical readers commonly identify her with Mary Lamb, Charles's sister, but the essay does not pause to explain the equation. The return to Bridget places the dream of marriage and children beside the continuing reality of the bachelor armchair and the domestic bond represented by her presence.

The ending is not a simple report of despair or acceptance. Its force comes from the abrupt reclassification of the scene: the children are dreams, the remembered brother is gone, and Bridget remains unchanged beside the waking narrator. Lamb lets the domestic present survive, but he does not resolve the grief or convert the lost future into a consoling lesson.
## The Prose of the Reverie

Formally, "Dream-Children" is structured as a single, long paragraph that flows without a break from the opening sentence to the final awakening. This lack of paragraph breaks is a deliberate formal choice: it mimics the movement of the dream, where one memory slides into another without the structural hinges of logical prose.

The language is characterized by its liquid, musical quality, its use of repetition and parallel clauses to create a hypnotic rhythm: "I told them how...", "I told them how...". This parallel structure draws the reader into the reverie, making the reading experience itself a kind of dream from which we are suddenly awakened at the end.

The form's achievement is internal rather than a claim of direct literary influence. Its long, unbroken movement lets memory, speech, and visual perception pass into one another, while the final awakening retrospectively changes the status of everything that came before. The prose represents the movements of desire and grief without naming them as a clinical psychology or assigning the essay a demonstrable priority in the later dream-vision tradition.
## The Empty Chair

The essay leaves the reader not with an empty chair but with the bachelor armchair occupied by the waking narrator and accompanied by the faithful Bridget. The dream-children are gone, while the final parenthesis removes John L., or James Elia, from the scene.

"Dream-Children" remains powerful because it refuses to turn the unlived life into a completed moral. The essay holds together the remembered house, the dead brother, the rejected courtship, and the imagined children, then returns them to a present that is materially small but emotionally unresolved. Its final achievement is to make the act of recollection itself feel like both consolation and renewed loss.

chapters.title: 30. Charles Lamb: "A Dissertation Upon Roast Pig"

content.value: Charles Lamb

**Original title:** "A Dissertation Upon Roast Pig" (first published in *The London Magazine*, September 1822; later collected in *Essays of Elia*, 1823)  
**Date:** 1822 CE  
**Original language:** English  
**Country/tradition:** England  
**Period/movement:** Romanticism; Cockney School  
**Genre:** Personal essay; familiar essay; mock-heroic dissertation; culinary satire

"Mankind, says a Chinese manuscript, which my friend M. was obliging enough to read and explain to me, for the first seventy thousand ages ate their meat raw, clawing or biting it from the living animal, just as they do in Abyssinia to this day." With this mock-scholarly attribution, Charles Lamb begins "A Dissertation Upon Roast Pig," published in *The London Magazine* in September 1822. The text names the translator only as M.; identifying that figure with Thomas Manning belongs to biographical conjecture, not to the essay's explicit evidence. The opening moves from the fantastic scale of seventy thousand ages to the immediate pleasures of eating.

This fictional manuscript is the pressure point of the essay. The story of Bo-bo, the swineherd's son who accidentally burns his father's cottage and discovers the taste of crackling, parodies solemn accounts of the origins of useful arts. Lamb's own joke points to a sage "like our Locke," who discovers that meat can be cooked without consuming a whole house. The essay replaces a dignified history of progress with an absurd chain of accident, appetite, imitation, and practical refinement.
## The Comedy of the Burnt Cottage

The narrative of Bo-bo and his father, Ho-ti, is told with the energy and physical comedy of a pantomime. Bo-bo is a simple boy, left in charge of the cottage while his father is out gathering mast. A spark falls into the straw, the cottage is burned to the ground, and a litter of nine new-farrowed pigs is roasted in the ruins:

> "Bo-bo was in the utmost consternation, not so much for the loss of the hut, which was a simple structure of wood and thatch, as for the fate of the pigs. He went searching among the smoking ruins, and his hand touched one of the burnt creatures. It felt hot, and some of the skin adhered to his fingers. He put his fingers to his mouth to cool them, and immediately tasted the crackling."

The description of the taste is the turning point of the narrative. Bo-bo does not weep for the cottage or the pigs; he begins to devour the meat with a wild, animal pleasure. When his father returns and begins to beat him for his carelessness, Bo-bo responds by thrusting a piece of the burnt pig into Ho-ti's mouth. The father’s anger dissolves at the first taste of the crackling: "The father and the son fell to together, devouring the remains of the litter, without any care for the house that had been lost."

The comedy is double-edged. It mocks the family's indifference to the destroyed cottage, but it also suggests that sensory pleasure can interrupt the authority of punishment, property, and inherited custom. The discovery becomes social only when appetite is repeated by the father, the neighbours, the court, and finally the wider district.

Soon, the secret escapes to the neighbors, and a rash of fires breaks out across the country: "Nothing was to be seen but fires in every village; the people shut up their kitchens, and began to burn down their own houses to roast their pigs, until at last a philosopher arose who showed them that the meat could be cooked in a common oven without the need for an arson."

This resolution parodies technological progress by turning an accidental discovery into a sequence of increasingly efficient methods. The sage does not cancel the appetite for roast pig; he separates the desired result from the destructive accident that first produced it.
## The Sensory Praise of the Pig

The second half of the essay is a direct, lyric celebration of the roast pig, in which the persona of Elia shifts from the mock-historian to the active gourmet. He describes the pig in terms that are almost erotic in their intensity:

> "There is no flavor comparable to that of the crisp, tawny, well-watched crackling of a roast pig. It is not fat; it is the fat; it is the essence of sweetness, the melting of the animal spirits into a physical form. The meat is tender, delicate, and sweet, like the flesh of a child."

The comparison with the innocence of the child-pig is a deliberately shocking turn in the praise. Lamb is not recommending cannibalism; he is personifying the animal's tenderness and using the language of moral innocence to intensify the epicure's appetite.
The pig, Elia argues, is the perfect food because it has no moral character:
> "The pig is a beast that is innocent of all labor; he does not plow the field or guard the gate; he lives only to eat and to be eaten. He is a gift of nature, designed for our delight."

This lack of mixed moral character is what makes the pig aesthetically superior within Elia's comic argument. Unlike humanity, which is a bundle of virtues and vices, the pig is presented as "good throughout," an image of shared fare and uncomplicated appetite. He becomes a culinary equivalent of the familiar essay: apparently useless in an administrative sense, but capable of refreshing the spirits.
## The Ethics of the Gift
The essay concludes with a reflection on the ethics of giving and sharing food. Elia admits that he freely shares many delicacies with his friends, but he makes an exception for roast pig:

> "I have a confession to make. I am not a hero. I can give away my coat; I can give away my money; but when a friend sends me a roast pig, I want to keep it for myself. To give away a pig is to commit a violence against my own appetite."

This confession undercuts the decorum of exemplary generosity from inside the persona. Elia is willing to laugh at his own boundary: he can distribute many good things, but he treats pig as a blessing specially adapted to his individual palate.

This selfishness is not presented as a moral failure, but as a natural human limit. The pleasure of taste is individual, not collective; you cannot eat a pig by deputy, and the satisfaction of your own stomach is a physical reality that resists the claims of altruism. By acknowledging this limit with a laugh, Lamb makes his narrator more human, showing that the good life is built on the honest acceptance of our appetites rather than the pursuit of impossible virtues.
## The Mock-Heroic Style

Formally, "A Dissertation Upon Roast Pig" is a mock-heroic performance, using elevated vocabulary, learned allusion, grand comparison, and legal or scholarly frames to describe a low and pleasurable subject.

Lamb uses Latinate terms and mock-scholarly phrases, invokes classical and biblical registers, and compares the essay's culinary discovery with the progress of useful arts. The most pointed comparison presents the sage who invents the gridiron as "like our Locke":
> "Bo-bo was the Prometheus of the kitchen: he brought down the fire of crackling to a raw-eating world, and in doing so, he did more for human happiness than all the philosophers of Greece."

This grand comparison is not just a joke; it shows how the essay borrows the prestige of philosophy in order to dignify a bodily pleasure. Lamb's learned manner does not elevate roast pig into an abstract principle. It makes the low subject capable of carrying argument, satire, appetite, and self-exposure at once.

The style is also characterized by its use of sensory adjectives: "crisp," "tawny," "crackling," "tender," "sweet," "melting." The language is designed to make the reader's mouth water, translating the physical sensation of eating into the rhythm of the prose.
## The Fire in the Hearth

The essay does not end with a narrated fireside dinner. It ends with Elia's comic refusal to distribute the pig he has reserved for his own palate, after which the prose turns to the practical question of sauce and seasoning. The mock history therefore returns to appetite as a personal act rather than a public moral.

"A Dissertation Upon Roast Pig" remains compelling because it makes bodily pleasure carry the full weight of literary form. The essay refuses to separate appetite from learning, morality, generosity, or vanity. Its cottage fire, mock trial, philosophical sage, epicurean description, and selfish confession all belong to the same comic argument: pleasure is neither outside thought nor reducible to a lesson about virtue.
Charles Lamb

**Original title:** "Old China" (first published in *The London Magazine*, March 1823; later collected in *Last Essays of Elia*, 1833)  
**Date:** 1823 CE  
**Original language:** English  
**Country/tradition:** England  
**Period/movement:** Romanticism; Cockney School  
**Genre:** Personal essay; familiar essay; domestic dialogue

"I have an almost feminine partiality for old china. When I go to see any great house, I inquire for the china-closet, and next for the picture-gallery." With this declaration of his "feminine partiality," Charles Lamb, writing under the persona of Elia, begins "Old China," published in *The London Magazine* in March 1823. The essay turns from a set of old blue china to the figures that seem to float, disregard distance, and inhabit a world before ordinary perspective. Its opening interest is not a general history of empire or commerce, but the way a domestic object releases a comic alternative to ordinary visual order.

This ornamental world is the pressure point of the essay. Elia is sitting at his tea-table with his cousin Bridget, whom biographical and editorial traditions identify with Mary Lamb, when their conversation turns from porcelain to the circumstances of their lives. Bridget observes that when they were poor, purchases required debate, saving, and shared effort, whereas greater comfort has diminished the drama of acquisition. By giving Bridget the long speech on the "pleasures of poverty," Lamb investigates the relationship between material difficulty and aesthetic response without reducing the argument to a general law of wealth.
## The Monologue of Bridget: The Pleasures of Poverty
The center of the essay is Bridget's extended speech. She recalls the specific sacrifices they made when money was scarce to buy books, prints, food, and theatre tickets:

> "I wish the good old times would come again, when we were not quite so rich. For then we had some pleasure in our lives. Do you remember the old folio of Beaumont and Fletcher that you bought at the bookstall in Covent Garden? You had eyed it for weeks, and when you finally decided to buy it, you had to walk home in the dark with the heavy volume under your arm, thinking of the coat you had to wear a little longer to pay for it."

The memory of the Beaumont and Fletcher folio makes acquisition into a narrative of attention. The value of the book is inseparable from the weeks of hesitation, the consultation of the purse, the worn suit, the late purchase, and the physical work of collating and repairing it. Lamb does not say that price determines value in every case; he dramatizes how effort can intensify attachment.

Bridget recalls other sacrifices: the time they walked miles in the rain to sit in the cheap gallery of the theater, wet and crowded, but full of excitement, while the rich people in the boxes looked bored and cold; the print of Leonardo da Vinci that they bought after saving for months; the wild strawberries they bought as a rare luxury at the end of the season.

These purchases were "adventures" because they required a choice. The worn suit, the shillings spent on a print, the shared food on country walks, and the one-shilling gallery all turn pleasure into a negotiated event. Now that Elia and Bridget can buy more easily, the older intensity has faded into convenience, at least in Bridget's recollection:

> "Now we can buy whatever we want without any trouble. We can go to the theater whenever we please, and sit in the best seats. But we do not enjoy the play as we did when we had to walk through the rain to get to the gallery."
## The Economy of Desire

Bridget's critique can be compared with later economic accounts of diminishing marginal utility, but that modern term should not be mistaken for Lamb's own framework. Her point is experiential: a shilling matters differently when it must be weighed against a coat, a book, a meal, or a theatre seat. The pleasure comes from the felt relation between desire, means, and effort.

Lamb applies this logic to aesthetic life. The essay suggests that taste, the capacity to receive pleasure from art, literature, food, and theatre, can be sharpened by difficulty and frequency can blunt attention. It does not establish that easy access always produces *ennui*; it stages Bridget's complaint and lets Elia answer it.

The people Bridget remembers as just above poverty work and plan for their pleasures. They walk to galleries and country places, save for a print, repair a book, and share what they can carry. The "pleasures of poverty" are therefore not an endorsement of deprivation. They are the pleasures of desire, the feeling of attention expanding around a small luxury that has been earned, debated, and shared.

This view of aesthetic value puts pressure on the language of comfort and acquisition, but it does not amount to a documented sociology of London's rising middle class. Lamb keeps the argument intimate. A purchase may become meaningful through hesitation, use, memory, and companionship, while abundance can make even a beautiful object feel ordinary.
## The Return to the Tea-Cup

After Bridget finishes her monologue, Elia responds with a qualified defence of their present situation. He admits that they had been happier when poorer, but reminds her that they were also younger and that their earlier struggles helped strengthen their compact.
But he insists that they must accept the present:

> "It is true, Bridget. We cannot return to the old times, and the wealth we have accumulated has brought its own burdens. But we must not be ungrateful. The tea is still hot, the china is still beautiful, and we are still here to drink it together."

The return to the physical reality of the tea-table is the essay's qualified conclusion. Nostalgia and the loss of youth are acknowledged, but Elia refuses to treat present competence as pure corruption. The dialogue ends by holding age, comfort, memory, and companionship in the same frame.

The old china becomes the object through which this tension is held. Its figures seem to float, while the conversation around it remains grounded in worn clothes, income, walks, plays, and age. The porcelain does not erase ordinary time, but it gives Elia a visual language for imagining distance, likeness, and pleasure outside the strict measurements of the household account.
## The Double Style of the Dialogue

Formally, "Old China" is structured as a dialogue between two voices: the nostalgic, critical voice of Bridget and the realistic, consolatory voice of Elia. This double structure allows Lamb to present both sides of the question of wealth and aging without resolving them too quickly.

The language moves from the elevated, playful description of porcelain to the detailed vocabulary of memory in the middle, including folios, coats, galleries, walks, strawberries, and peas, then returns to a reflective domestic image. The conversation feels intimate because the objects and places are shared, not because the essay supplies a complete chronology of the speakers' life together.

The conversational style makes a philosophical problem feel domestic without ceasing to be an argument. Bridget's rhetoric expands from a cup to a theory of desire, and Elia's reply brings the theory back to age, competence, and shared history. The essay's formal achievement lies in that alternation rather than in a claim that it established a single later standard for English prose.
## The Empty Cup

The essay leaves the reader with the two cousins still at the table, looking again at a small Chinese figure holding an umbrella over a lady in a blue summer-house. The argument has not emptied the cups or dissolved the past; it has returned the speakers to the object that first made their disagreement visible.

"Old China" remains powerful because it refuses to resolve nostalgia into either moralising or sentimentality. The past cannot be recovered, yet the present is not simply a poor substitute for youth. Through the tea-table dialogue, Lamb shows how an object can preserve an old pleasure while also exposing the changes in money, age, and companionship that make that pleasure intelligible.
Charles Lamb

**Original title:** "The Superannuated Man" (first published in *The London Magazine*, May 1825; later collected in *Last Essays of Elia*, 1833)  
**Date:** 1825 CE  
**Original language:** English  
**Country/tradition:** England  
**Period/movement:** Romanticism; Cockney School  
**Genre:** Personal essay; familiar essay; reflection on retirement

"If peradventure, Reader, it has been thy lot to waste the golden years of thy life, thy shining youth, in the study of law-books, or in the dry calculations of a merchant’s ledger, thou wilt know the weight of that chain which I have dragged for thirty-six years." With this direct address to the reader, Charles Lamb, writing under the persona of Elia, begins "The Superannuated Man," published in *The London Magazine* in May 1825. The essay presents the chain as the life of a clerk, six and thirty years at a desk in Mincing-lane and eight, nine, or ten hours a day in a counting-house. Biographical notes connect the disguised employment with Lamb's East India House service, but the essay itself preserves the fiction of a firm and its partners.

This administrative labor is the pressure point of the essay. The fictional narrator describes a sudden release after six and thirty years, while biographical records place Lamb's real retirement from the East India House on 29 March 1825 and record a pension proposal with differing figures in the surrounding documentation. The essay should therefore be read as a shaped account of emancipation, not as a verbatim institutional record. By analysing the expansion of time and the difficulty of adjusting to life without office work, Lamb investigates the relation between employment, time, and identity through the language of captivity and release.
## The Prison of the Desk and the Six Days of Labor

The first movement of the essay is a description of the clerk's life, which is characterized by its monotony and its lack of connection to the natural world. Elia describes himself as a prisoner of the calendar:

> "My day was divided by the clock; my year by the holidays. I was like a horse in a mill, constantly turning the same wheel, without ever seeing the country or feeling the sun except through the windows of the office. The ledgers were my tombs, and my life was written in their figures."
The only relief from this monotony was the Sunday, which Elia describes as a day of complex, often unsatisfactory rest:

> "The Sunday was my only day of freedom, but it was a day of transition. I spent the morning preparing for the office, and the evening dreading its arrival. The day was too short for real rest; it was merely a pause in the turning of the wheel."

The description of the "mill" of labour belongs to the essay's rhetoric of captivity. It turns office routine, counting-house hours, Sundays, and annual holidays into a system of measured time. The biographical East India House context helps explain the personal resonance, but the chapter does not need to generalise from Lamb's experience to the whole of British imperial administration or to a modern history of white-collar work.

Lamb's critique is that this work ethic destroys the individual's capacity to experience time. The clerk's time is not his own; it is sold to the company, and the years pass in a blur of routine: "I have lived thirty-six years, but I have not had thirty-six years of life. My life has been spent in the service of others, and my own time has been limited to the evenings and the holidays."
## The Gift of Retirement and the Shock of Freedom
The transition to retirement arrives suddenly, like a miracle in the narrator's account:

> "On the evening of the twelfth of April, I was called into the chamber of the directors. I went with a heavy heart, believing that my health was to be inspected and my salary reduced. Instead, they told me that I was to be retired, with a pension of two-thirds of his salary. I walked out of the office a free man."
This sudden gift is met not with immediate joy, but with shock and disorientation. Elia describes the first days of retirement as a period of temporal distortion:

> "I had too much time. The day lay before me like a vast, empty ocean, and I had no compass to guide me. I walked through the streets of London, looking at the busy people, and felt myself a ghost who had escaped from the grave. I did not know what to do with my hands."

This psychology of time's expansion is one of the deepest observations in the essay. The retired clerk is like a prisoner who has been released after decades of confinement: the walls are gone, but the habits of the cell remain. He is used to having his time organized by the clock, and the sudden absence of this structure makes him feel unstable, as if he were floating in the air.

He later visits his old desk-fellows and finds that the desk and the peg where he hung his hat have been appropriated by another. The business continues without him, and the scene combines remorse, vanity, affection, and relief. The institution that held his working life does not collapse when he leaves, but neither can he sever himself from its human attachments at once.
## The Master of Time and the Gentleman of Leisure
The second half of the essay records the narrator's adjustment to his new condition. He begins to learn a form of leisure in which time can be walked, read, or written at the moment of inclination:

> "I am now the master of my own hours. I can write when I please, read when I please, and walk when I please. I have become a gentleman of leisure, a member of the 'superannuated' class who have earned the right to do nothing."

Elia describes walking through London during the week, visiting book-stalls, looking at pictures, and observing the people still engaged in business. He is no longer moving only to and from the office. The new perspective is comic and self-conscious, mixing the freedom of observation with the vanity of imagining himself a gentleman of leisure.

This leisure is not presented simply as idleness. The retired man can walk, read, write, visit friends, and let pleasure arrive without having to compress it into a holiday. He has reclaimed a portion of time that the essay distinguishes from the hours lived for other people, although the narrator continues to acknowledge the strangeness and guilt of leaving his old companions.

The celebration of retirement is framed as a personal counter-value to office discipline, not as a documented survey of industrial attitudes. Lamb's narrator is deliberately extravagant when he wishes to abolish desks and cotton mills, and that exaggeration turns a private release into social satire without making the chapter a general history of industrial labour.
## The Prose of Leisure

Formally, the essay moves from an opening address and compressed history of office life into digression, anecdote, quotation, and self-correction. The syntax does not merely reproduce a timetable; it makes the expansion of time visible by allowing the narrator to wander through memory, London, books, friends, and philosophical fantasy.

The language of the first half is full of technical, administrative terms: "ledgers," "balances," "salaries," "pensions," "directors." The language of the second half is full of natural and literary imagery: "oceans," "mountains," "clocks," "gardens," "gentlemen." The transitions are slow, mirroring the gradual adjustment of the narrator's mind to his new freedom.

The style also uses classical and historical references to enlarge and mock the narrator's role. Virgil's liberty, the Bastille, Roman and literary allusions, and the language of eternity give a clerk's release a mock-heroic scale. The grandeur is deliberately unstable: the narrator is both a liberated captive and a man learning how to manage an ordinary day.
## The Quiet Hearth

The essay ends with Elia declaring that he is no longer a clerk but "Retired Leisure." He walks without a fixed purpose, reads the state of the opera, and says that he has done his task-work and has the rest of the day to himself. The ending is a verbal act of renaming rather than a scene of a stopped clock or a closed ledger.

"The Superannuated Man" remains compelling because it makes time itself the subject of a comic personal essay. Lamb holds together office fatigue, institutional gratitude, guilt toward former colleagues, the shock of freedom, and the pleasure of unstructured movement. The chain is broken, but the old desk-fellows and the habits of captivity remain in memory, which is why the essay's freedom feels earned, precarious, and human rather than absolute.
William Hazlitt

**Original title:** *Table-Talk; or, Original Essays*, Essay XXIV, "On Familiar Style"  
**Date:** 1821 CE  
**Original language:** English  
**Country/tradition:** England  
**Period/movement:** Romanticism; Cockney School  
**Genre:** Critical essay; treatise on prose style

"It is not easy to write a familiar style. Many people mistake a familiar for a vulgar style, and think that to write without affectation is to write at random. On the contrary, there is nothing that requires more precision, and, if I may so say, purity of expression, than the style I am speaking of." With this opening distinction, William Hazlitt begins "On Familiar Style," one of the most significant essays on writing in the English language, published in his 1821 collection *Table-Talk*.

This opening distinction is the pressure point of the essay. Hazlitt is writing during a period in English literary history when prose style was highly polarized: on the one hand, the "polite" world was dominated by the heavy, Latinate, and highly structured prose of Samuel Johnson and his imitators; on the other hand, the popular press was full of slang, vulgarisms, and careless writing. "On Familiar Style" is Hazlitt's attempt to define a middle way: a style that is natural, conversational, and direct, yet precise, elegant, and forceful. By analyzing the choices a writer must make to achieve this style, Hazlitt does not simply write a manual of composition; he articulates a democratic theory of language, arguing that the best prose is that which is grounded in the common speech of the people rather than the artificial codes of the court or the academy.
## The Definition of the Familiar
To write a familiar style, Hazlitt argues, is to write as you would speak in polite conversation with a friend:

> "To write a genuine familiar or truly English style, is to write as any one would speak in common conversation, who had a thorough command and choice of words, or who could discourse with ease, force, and perspicuity, setting aside all pedantic and systematic ornaments."

This definition is simple, but its execution is difficult. The writer must choose the words that are "natural" to the subject, avoiding both the "tall" words of the scholars and the "low" words of the street. Hazlitt compared this choice to the selection of a path: the writer must follow the main road of the language, without turning aside into the wilderness of pedantry or the ditch of vulgarity.

The familiar style is not a careless style. It does not allow the writer to write whatever enters his head without revision: "To write without affectation is not to write at random. On the contrary, it requires more precision to write in the common vocabulary than in any other, because the reader is a judge of the correctness of the copy; he knows immediately if a word is out of place."

In a pedantic style, the writer can hide his lack of thought under layers of long words and complex syntax; in the familiar style, the thought is exposed, and any weakness of logic or clarity becomes visible at once.
## The Critique of Pedantry and the Johnsonian School
The primary target of Hazlitt's critique is the style of Samuel Johnson, which he sees as the grand example of the pedantic and the artificial:

> "Dr. Johnson's style is like a machine: it turns out sentences of the same size, weight, and structure, without any reference to the variety of the subjects. He uses the same Latinate words and parallel structures to describe a moral crisis or a recipe for tea. The style is a mask that hides the character of the writer."

Hazlitt rejects this "Johnsonian" style because it destroys the individuality of the writer and the immediacy of the thought. The reader is not listening to a person; he is listening to a machine. The style is "monotonous," "heavy," and "academic," and its influence has been to corrupt English prose by making writers believe that to write well is to write as if they were translating from the Latin.
He is no less sharp on the "poetical" prose of his contemporaries, who filled their essays with metaphors, descriptions, and elevated language that had no connection to the argument:

> "They cannot write a simple statement without calling in the aid of the stars, the flowers, and the winds. Their prose is a garden of weeds, beautiful to look at but useless for any rational purpose. They have forgotten that the first duty of prose is to be clear."

This critique of ornament is a key Hazlitt principle. Style is not a decoration to be added to the thought; it is the physical form of the thought itself. The writer who uses too many metaphors is like a builder who covers his house with ornaments to hide the weakness of the walls.
## The Democratic Politics of Language

Hazlitt's defense of the familiar style is also a political statement. He was a radical writer, a defender of the French Revolution and the rights of the citizen, who spent his career challenging the authority of the Tory government and the aristocratic institutions of Britain.

In "On Familiar Style," he connects the hierarchy of style to the hierarchy of class. The pedantic, Latinate style is the language of the court, the university, and the church, institutions that used their specialized vocabularies to exclude the common people from the public sphere. By writing in a style that was difficult and artificial, they maintained their authority, presenting their opinions as universal truths that only the learned could understand.

The familiar style, by contrast, is the language of the citizen. It is the language of the market, the tavern, and the parlor, accessible to anyone who has common sense and a basic education. By writing in this style, Hazlitt challenges the intellectual authority of the ruling class: he shows that the most profound questions of literature, philosophy, and politics can be discussed in the common vocabulary of the people, without the need for academic credentials or aristocratic patrons.

This democratic view of language was central to the Cockney School's project. Hazlitt, Lamb, and Hunt were trying to build a new, inclusive public sphere, where the clerk, the merchant, and the writer could meet as equals around the table of the daily press.
## The Prose of Force and Movement

Formally, Hazlitt's own style in the essay is the perfect demonstration of his theory. It is a style of extraordinary energy, speed, and force, which differs from both the dry calculations of Bacon and the quiet melancholy of Lamb.

Hazlitt's sentences are long, flowing, and cumulative, but they are held together by a strong, logical rhythm that keeps them from falling into confusion. He uses active verbs, concrete nouns, and direct address to keep the reader engaged:
> "We do not want to be lectured; we want to be spoken to. The writer who knows his art will treat his reader as a companion, not as a student."

He uses a variety of rhetorical devices to maintain this conversational energy: he asks questions, anticipates objections, quotes contemporary slang, and cites classical sources, all within the same paragraph. The transitions are quick, the language is dense, and the metaphors are drawn from the physical world, paths, roads, machines, gardens, clothes.

This material vocabulary is important. By describing style in terms of physical movement and physical choices, Hazlitt makes the art of writing look like a practical skill, a craft to be learned through discipline and attention rather than a mysterious gift of the muses.
## The Open Road of the Language

The essay concludes with a warning against the dangers of imitation. Hazlitt notes that the writer who tries to write in the style of another will always fail, because style must be the expression of the writer's own character:

> "Let no man write like Johnson, or like Addison, or like myself. Let him write like himself. The familiar style is not a template; it is a path that each writer must cut for himself through the forest of the language."

This warning is the final qualified conclusion. There is no simple rule for the familiar style; there is no dictionary of acceptable words or manual of correct syntax. The writer must rely on his own ear, his own judgment, and his own commitment to truth. The open road of the language is there, the path is difficult, and the journey must be conducted by oneself. Hazlitt has shown us the direction; the walk belongs to the reader.
William Hazlitt

**Original title:** *Table-Talk; or, Original Essays*, Essay IX, "The Indian Jugglers"  
**Date:** 1821 CE  
**Original language:** English  
**Country/tradition:** England  
**Period/movement:** Romanticism; Cockney School  
**Genre:** Personal essay; critical reflection; aesthetic essay

"Coming forward and sitting down on the ground in his worn, dark dress, the Indian juggler began his performance by taking four brass balls and throwing them into the air. He kept them moving in a circle with the speed and precision of a machine, never dropping one, never hesitation, for several minutes." With this description of a street performance in London, William Hazlitt begins "The Indian Jugglers," one of the most famous essays in his 1821 collection *Table-Talk*.

This performance is the pressure point of the essay. The sight of the juggler keeping the four brass balls in the air with perfect precision is not merely an entertainment; it is a challenge to the writer’s vanity. Hazlitt, who spent his life writing essays, reviews, and pamphlets in a style that was always contested, always subject to error, and always incomplete, is struck by the juggler’s absolute mastery of his craft. The juggler does not fail; he does not make excuses; he simply performs a task that is difficult with perfect, unrepeatable success. By analyzing the difference between this physical dexterity and the intellectual and artistic achievements of the writer, the painter, and the statesman, Hazlitt investigates the nature of greatness, showing that the highest human efforts are often those that are most subject to failure.
## The Perfection of the Juggler and the Failure of the Writer
Hazlitt's first reaction to the juggler is a feeling of personal insignificance:

> "It makes me sad to look at him. He does something that is difficult with perfect success, and he does it every time. I spend my life trying to write a sentence or formulate an idea, and I am always failing. My words are always inadequate, my thoughts are always incomplete, and my readers are always ready to tell me I am wrong."

The contrast is between the certainty of the physical and the uncertainty of the intellectual. The juggler operates in a world of physical laws: gravity, momentum, eye-hand coordination. The test of his success is simple: either the ball is caught or it falls. There is no room for interpretation, no debate about the quality of the performance, no factional interest that can argue the ball was not caught.

The writer, by contrast, operates in a world of language, opinion, and value. The test of his success is complex, subjective, and always delayed. He can write a sentence that he believes is beautiful and true, and find that his readers find it obscure or false. He is always negotiating with the limits of his medium, trying to represent experiences that resist translation into words.

This difference produces a difference in the quality of the achievement. The juggler has achieved *perfection* at the expense of *scale*. His task is narrow, mechanical, and does not engage the moral or emotional life of the spectator. The writer's task is vast, complex, and seeks to address the deepest questions of human existence; and because the task is so large, the writer must always fail to achieve the absolute completeness that the juggler exhibits with his brass balls.
## Cavanagh and the Genius of the Fives-Court

To expand this inquiry into the nature of physical perfection, Hazlitt introduces a second character: John Cavanagh, the celebrated Irish fives-player who had recently died. Cavanagh was a house-painter by trade, but at the fives-court in St. Martin’s Street, he was an artist of unrepeatable genius:

> "When he touched the ball, there was a silent, sudden force that sent it exactly where he wanted it to go. He did not seem to run or exert himself; he was always in the right place, his eye and his hand working together with the same certainty that the Indian juggler exhibits with his brass balls. He was the Shakespeare of the fives-court."

Hazlitt's description of Cavanagh’s play is characterized by its kinetic energy. He describes the sound of the ball against the wall, the grace of Cavanagh’s movement, and the despair of his opponents, who found themselves defeated by a style that looked simple but was impossible to imitate. Cavanagh's game was a combination of strength, speed, and absolute precision: he could place the ball in the corners of the court with such accuracy that it was unreachable, or hit it with such force that it died on the floor.

Yet this athletic genius, like the juggler’s skill, has left nothing behind it but memory. Cavanagh died in poverty, his name unknown to the general public, his achievement recorded only in the recollections of the people who watched him play. The house-painter who was a king in St. Martin’s Street is now a handful of dust, and his genius has vanished with the movement of his arm.

This transience is the tragedy of the physical artist. The actor, the dancer, the singer, and the athlete can achieve a perfection that is denied to the writer or the painter, but their art is tethered to the moment of its performance. When the body fails, the art dies; the spectator is left with nothing but the recollection of a motion that can never be repeated.
## The Hierarchy of Achievement: Juggler, Painter, Poet, Statesman
To analyze these differences systematically, Hazlitt constructs a hierarchy of human activities based on the relationship between skill and value.

At the bottom is the juggler or the acrobat, whose achievement is entirely physical and mechanical. It requires years of discipline, but it does not require the cultivation of the intellect or the sympathy of the heart: "The juggler's skill is a dead thing; it has no moral character and leaves nothing behind it but the memory of a trick."
Above the juggler is the craftsman or the mechanic, whose skill is also physical but has a practical utility: the builder, the weaver, the watchmaker.

Above the craftsman is the painter or the sculptor, whose work combines physical dexterity with intellectual design. The painter must know how to mix colors, manage perspective, and handle the brush, but he must also have a vision of the world, a capacity to see and represent the character of his subject. Hazlitt, who had trained as a portrait painter in his youth, knew the difficulty of this combination: the hand must execute what the eye sees, and the eye must see what is hidden below the surface.

At the summit is the poet or the philosopher, whose work is entirely intellectual and emotional. The poet does not rely on the physical dexterity of the hand; he relies on the capacity of language to evoke response. His medium is the most unstable of all, yet his achievement is the most durable: the words of Shakespeare or Milton remain long after the watchmaker's watch has stopped and the painter's canvas has faded.

Finally, Hazlitt considers the statesman or the warrior, whose achievement is measured by its effect on the history of the world. He is particularly sharp on the figure of the general, whose "greatness" is often a matter of accident and the sacrifice of others:

> "The general who wins a battle is called great, but his greatness is often the work of his soldiers, the mistakes of his enemy, or the direction of the wind. He does not control the elements of his success as the juggler controls his balls."

This critique of military glory is a key Hazlitt position. He had watched the rise and fall of Napoleon Bonaparte, whom he admired as a destroyer of the old feudal order, but whose ultimate failure demonstrated the instability of military power. The general's victory is temporary; the poet's victory is permanent.
## The Style of the Spectator

Formally, "The Indian Jugglers" is structured as a transition from the tavern performance at the beginning to a historical and critical reflection in the middle, and back to a personal confession at the end.

The language of the first half is visual, concrete, and physical: the brass balls, the dark dress, the speed of the hand, the sound of the catch. The language of the second half is abstract, philosophical, and critical, using the vocabulary of aesthetic theory (skill, genius, greatness, utility).

The style is characterized by its use of contrasts and balanced assertions: the perfection of the hand vs. the failure of the mind; the narrowness of the trick vs. the scale of the poem; the certainty of gravity vs. the uncertainty of opinion. These contrasts structure the argument, giving the prose a logical tension that matches the tension of the juggler's performance.

Yet the essay is not a dry treatise. Hazlitt's voice remains personal, opinionated, and responsive throughout. He is not a scholar writing from a library; he is a spectator writing from a tavern, his mind stimulated by the sights and sounds of the street.
## The Unresolved Struggle
The essay concludes with a return to the narrator's own work. He is sitting at his desk, the paper lies before him, and he must begin the next sentence.

"The Indian Jugglers" remains a classic because it is one of the deepest reflections on the limits of human achievement in our literature. Hazlitt refuses the easy consolations of self-congratulation. He knows that his writing is imperfect, and that he will never achieve the clean, machine-like success of the street performer or the fives-player. But he also knows that the search for the impossible, the attempt to represent the complexity of our nature in the shifting sand of language, is the only work that is worthy of a rational being. The juggler has caught his balls, the fives-court in St. Martin’s Street is empty, and the writer is left alone with his pen.
William Hazlitt

**Original title:** "On Going a Journey"  
**Date:** 1822  
**Original language:** English  
**Country/tradition:** England  
**Period/movement:** Romantic period; familiar essay  
**Genre:** Personal essay; travel reflection

William Hazlitt wants to walk without having to explain himself. The request sounds modest, but "On Going a Journey" makes it the basis of an inquiry into attention, friendship, memory, and the difficulty of sharing experience. Published in the *New Monthly Magazine* in January 1822 and collected in the second volume of *Table-Talk* that year, the essay begins with a preference for solitary travel. Its movement gradually exposes the limits of that preference. A walk can release the traveller from familiar obligations, yet the mind carries a crowded history into its apparent solitude. The essay's solitary speaker remains dependent on books, remembered voices, and imagined listeners.

The opening puts a personal qualification beside a general pleasure. Travelling is agreeable; travelling alone is what Hazlitt particularly likes. This distinction matters because the essay never acquires the authority of a universal prescription. Its argument proceeds through the temperament of a recognisable speaker. His impatience is part of his appeal, and his willingness to discover exceptions keeps that impatience from hardening into a rule for everyone. The reader follows a preference being tested in prose.
## The labour of explaining a sensation

Companionship divides attention. Hazlitt cannot fully surrender to a passing association while attending to the responses of another person. A landscape may recall something intimate that a companion cannot understand without a laborious explanation. The difficulty concerns the timing of expression. What can become an essay afterwards may be damaged by compulsory conversation at the moment of perception.

Hazlitt therefore distinguishes receiving impressions from analysing them. He wants to accumulate sensations before examining their connections. This distinction also describes the conditions of his own writing. The essay gives articulate shape to experiences whose original pleasure depended upon freedom from articulation. Its fluency is retrospective. The apparent contradiction between an eloquent defence of silence and the silence defended becomes a productive account of composition: experience needs an interval before it becomes communicable.

His humorous complaints prevent this account from becoming solemn. A companion may fail to smell a field or need spectacles to see an object. Such small mismatches make sympathy inconvenient without making the companion morally deficient. The comedy catches the unreasonable wish that another person should duplicate one's senses. Hazlitt acknowledges his own pleasure in argument while asking for temporary release from it. Solitude permits him to leave conclusions undefended, a privilege the essay's readers are under no obligation to grant him.
## Books and voices on the road

The supposedly unaccompanied walk contains many literary companions. Quotations and allusions interrupt the prose, giving remembered language an active role in perception. Nature does not appear as an experience untouched by culture. It awakens phrases already stored in the traveller's mind. The literary texture complicates any claim that Hazlitt simply opposes books to landscape or intellect to bodily sensation.

Coleridge provides a still more direct exception. Hazlitt recalls a speaker whose conversation could transform scenery into imaginative language without making it tedious. The recollection measures the difference between ordinary conversational obligation and an extraordinary capacity to communicate. It also introduces loss. The desired voice belongs to an earlier companionship that cannot simply be restored by choosing to walk together again.

Lamb offers a comic counterpart. Hazlitt suggests that the qualities making him excellent indoor company make him unsuitable outdoors. The distinction is situational, not a verdict against friendship. A form of talk has its proper setting. The essay's title in *Table-Talk* consequently acquires a small irony: an indoor literary performance explains when conversation should stop.
## The inn and the remembered self

The prospect of supper qualifies the ban on conversation before the traveller reaches his destination. Appetite offers a subject that companions can enjoy discussing. Hazlitt's imagined dishes and anticipated shelter give thought a bodily setting. Walking changes the value of ordinary comforts by producing the hunger and fatigue that make them welcome.

At the inn, anonymity allows a suspension of social identity. The traveller can temporarily escape the expectations attached to his name. Yet Hazlitt also remembers reading there, solving an intellectual problem, and looking at pictures. The inn does not empty the mind. It makes room for activities released from their usual setting and urgency. Its freedom depends on an interval within ordinary life.

The recollection of Llangollen deepens this account. Hazlitt remembers an evening associated with Rousseau's *New Eloise*, food and wine, the Welsh landscape, and the expectations of youth. Sensory details anchor an experience whose emotional force exceeds the objects described. The valley recalls a former confidence in human possibility. Returning to it would mean encountering the distance between that earlier consciousness and the present speaker.

Here solitude protects grief as much as pleasure. Another person cannot occupy precisely the same relation to the remembered place. Hazlitt's wish to return alone follows from the singularity of his associations, rather than from a general contempt for human company. His memory also disturbs the promise of self-escape. The journey that loosens the present identity can bring an earlier identity painfully close.
## The changing scale of the imagination

Hazlitt moves from reminiscence into an argument about the mind's limited capacity. A new scene displaces the scene just left. Physical movement changes the immediate scale of importance, making the visible surroundings seem disproportionately comprehensive. This is an observation about situated consciousness, not evidence that travelling automatically broadens judgement.

His account gives forgetting a role alongside recollection. Places can revive forgotten feelings, but the mind cannot retain every place with equal vividness at once. The essay itself responds to this limitation through succession. It turns from road to inn, from recollection to reflection, allowing one scene to prompt another. Its digressions enact the associative process under discussion. They are structurally necessary to an argument about experience arriving in partial views.

The prose repeatedly returns to its abandoned question. These returns make its looseness intelligible. Hazlitt can appear to wander because the reader retains the originating preference against which each excursion is measured. The familiar essay accommodates psychological complexity without converting experience into a fixed sequence of propositions.
## The exceptions that make the ending

Near the close, Hazlitt explicitly welcomes companions for visits to ruins, pictures, and other objects that support discussion. Foreign travel presents another qualification: familiar speech and fellowship can become consolations when ordinary associations are absent. He then remembers France with an enthusiasm that unsettles even this exception. Personal experience repeatedly exceeds the explanatory rule just proposed.

The ending therefore does not simply return a refreshed walker to a London desk. It considers the strange separation of foreign experience from habitual existence, then imagines having one life for travelling and another for home. The wish cannot be fulfilled. Its impossibility gives the essay its final measure of freedom. Travel offers valuable changes of consciousness, but the traveller cannot possess all possible lives simultaneously. Hazlitt's achievement lies in making this limit felt through the changing movement of an individual voice.
## Sources and textual notes

William Hazlitt, "On Going a Journey", *New Monthly Magazine*, January 1822; *Table-Talk*, volume II, 1822. Primary text: [University of Alberta transcription](<https://sites.ualberta.ca/~dmiall/Travel/hazlitt.htm>). Publication corroboration: [British Library manuscript catalogue, Add MS 61732](<https://searcharchives.bl.uk/catalog/032-001961941>). Commentary refers to the essay's narrated memories without treating their autobiographical details as independently established events. No direct quotations from the essay are reproduced here.

chapters.title: 36. William Hazlitt: "On the Pleasure of Hating"

content.value: William Hazlitt

**Original title:** "On the Pleasure of Hating"  
**Date:** 1826, collected in *The Plain Speaker*  
**Original language:** English  
**Country/tradition:** England  
**Period/movement:** Romantic period; familiar essay  
**Genre:** Personal and moral essay

A spider crosses the floor of the room in which William Hazlitt is sitting. He allows it to escape, but his restraint does not remove his disgust. "On the Pleasure of Hating", collected in *The Plain Speaker* in 1826, develops from this uncomfortable difference between humane action and hostile feeling. The opening is carefully chosen. Hazlitt neither kills the creature nor congratulates himself without qualification. The essay begins where a reassuring narrative of moral progress might have ended, with the discovery that civil behaviour can coexist with an imagination still governed by aversion.

The title promises a scandalous pleasure, but the essay does not offer a straightforward recommendation to hate. Its speaker investigates a source of energy that he recognises in himself. His examples widen from an involuntary response to a spider into public entertainments, religious hostility, patriotism, broken friendships, reading, and political disappointment. This widening movement eventually returns judgement to the person making it. The authority of the essay depends upon the writer's refusal to remain safely outside his subject.
## The survival of an impulse

The spider establishes two different measures of civilisation. One concerns conduct: the creature survives because the observer restrains himself. The other concerns sentiment: dislike persists after violence has been rejected. Hazlitt refuses to make the survival of feeling cancel the value of restraint. Yet restraint alone cannot justify confidence that hostility has disappeared. A society may become less openly cruel while preserving the appetites that once sustained cruelty.

This distinction gives the essay a psychological focus. Hatred supplies excitement, sharpens contrast, and creates objects on which restless feeling can settle. Hazlitt's sweeping formulations should be read as provocative moral generalisations, not as experimentally established laws of human behaviour. Their extremity exposes possibilities that respectable self-description tends to conceal. The questions he poses about pride, envy, and malice leave the explanation unsettled even while his examples accumulate.

The prose makes that accumulation pleasurable. An aphorism gives way to an anecdote, then to a grotesque image or sudden question. Readers enjoy the performance through which enjoyment of hostility is being examined. This involvement is more effective than a denunciation delivered from an untroubled moral height. The essay lets its own wit become evidence of the difficulty it describes.
## Public amusement and moral disguise

Hazlitt turns to spectators who gather around fires, crimes, and executions. His point concerns the difference between approving an outcome and enjoying the excitement that precedes it.
