chapters.title: 100. Jia Tolentino: “The I in the Internet”

content.value: **Original title:** “The I in the Internet” **Date:** 2019 (collection appearance in *Trick Mirror: Reflections on Self-Delusion*) **Original language:** English **Country/tradition:** United States; contemporary digital culture criticism **Period/movement:** Twenty-first-century internet writing; feminist cultural criticism **Genre:** Personal essay; technology and identity criticism
## The self as a platform

Jia Tolentino’s “The I in the Internet” asks what happens to the self when online life turns identity into a public, searchable, and marketable object. The essay is not simply a complaint about distraction or social media manners. It is an inquiry into the conditions under which a person becomes visible. The internet promises connection and expression, but it also encourages the user to treat the self as a project whose value depends on circulation.

The title places the pronoun inside the network. The “I” is still personal, but it no longer appears alone. It is surrounded by platforms, audiences, metrics, images, recommendation systems, and inherited styles of self-presentation. Tolentino’s question is how much agency remains when the tools for expression also shape what can be expressed and what will be rewarded.

The essay’s personal dimension is essential because Tolentino does not write from outside the culture she describes. She has used the internet as a reader, writer, participant, and observer. Her critique includes her own habits and desires. This complicity gives the essay its credibility, but it also gives it its unease. The problem is not that other people are performing online while the writer remains authentic. Everyone is implicated, including the critic who turns participation into analysis.

Tolentino’s argument begins from a familiar experience: the self online can feel both more deliberate and less free than the self in physical life. A post can be edited, framed, and distributed to a chosen audience. It can also be copied, misread, ranked, and detached from its original context. The user gains a sense of authorship while entering systems that are designed to capture attention and produce data.
## Identity under observation

The internet changes the meaning of self-presentation because observation is continuous. A person does not merely appear before an audience and then leave the stage. The audience may be invisible, indefinite, or algorithmically assembled. The post remains available after the moment that produced it. The self therefore becomes a record of prior performances, each of which can be searched for evidence about who the person really is.

Tolentino is interested in the anxiety produced by this condition. The user must imagine how an unknown audience will interpret an image, sentence, or opinion. At the same time, the user is encouraged to make the self more legible. The platform rewards recognisable identity, consistent tone, and emotional immediacy. Complexity can be difficult to display because it does not always produce a quick response.

This is not only a psychological problem. It is a political economy. Platforms make money from attention, and attention is easier to capture when the user’s identity becomes part of the content. The personal post is not just an expression. It is also an object that can be sorted, promoted, targeted, and monetised. The user may feel that the platform is a tool for self-expression while the platform treats the user as a source of valuable behaviour.

Tolentino’s critique does not assume that every online act is false. An online identity may express real desire, real pain, and real political commitment. The point is that authenticity itself can be formatted. The platform can reward confessional language, outrage, vulnerability, or moral certainty. What feels spontaneous may have been shaped by years of observing which kinds of selfhood receive attention.
## The fantasy of escape

One of the essay’s recurrent concerns is the belief that the internet offers escape from older hierarchies. Digital culture often presents itself as open, participatory, and democratic. Anyone can publish, gather an audience, or invent a new identity. Tolentino acknowledges the genuine possibilities in that openness, especially for people who have been excluded from traditional institutions. Yet she also asks what happens when liberation is delivered through private platforms whose rules are opaque and whose incentives favour extraction.

The fantasy of escape can therefore reproduce the world it claims to leave behind. Popularity becomes a new form of status. Visibility becomes a new source of inequality. The users who appear to be freely expressing themselves may be responding to the demands of an attention market that distributes rewards unevenly. Even the language of individuality can serve a system that turns difference into a commodity.

This tension is especially important for feminist criticism. Online spaces can give women and marginalised people tools for testimony, solidarity, and collective action. They can also expose them to surveillance, harassment, sexualisation, and demands for endless emotional labour. Tolentino does not treat the internet as either emancipatory or oppressive in the abstract. She examines the contradictory ways its structure intensifies both possibilities.

The self is asked to be public enough to attract attention and controlled enough to remain acceptable. This is a difficult combination. A user may be expected to reveal personal experience while avoiding the forms of anger, ambiguity, or need that make the audience uncomfortable. The platform becomes a place where vulnerability is encouraged as content but discouraged as a demand for structural change.
## Attention and desire

The essay’s argument is also about desire. The internet is not powerful only because it traps users. It is powerful because it offers pleasures that are genuinely pleasurable. The feed can provide surprise, recognition, information, intimacy, and relief from boredom. A critique that ignores those pleasures becomes moralistic. Tolentino instead asks why the user keeps returning even after understanding the system’s costs.

Attention is the medium of the exchange. The user gives time and receives stimulation. Platforms make the exchange feel personal by learning preferences and delivering content that seems to know the user. The result is an intimate structure built from prediction. The user may experience the feed as a mirror, but the mirror is also a machine for shaping desire.

Tolentino’s first-person method keeps this analysis from becoming a simple denunciation. She is not claiming that knowledge produces immunity. The critic can recognise manipulation and still want to look. This is one of the essay’s most honest insights. The problem is not ignorance alone. It is that the system has become entangled with ordinary needs for belonging, distraction, and self-recognition.

The internet’s power also comes from its ability to collapse distances. Private feeling can become public speech almost instantly. A local event can become a shared reference. A person can enter a conversation that would otherwise be unavailable. These possibilities are meaningful, but they also make the boundary between experience and performance unstable. The user learns to feel through the categories that the network makes visible.
## The self as argument

Tolentino’s essay is not organised as a neutral report on technology. It is an argument about the political meaning of first person writing. When the self becomes the primary evidence, the writer gains immediacy but risks making structural conditions appear private. A person may feel isolated, anxious, or compulsive, while the cause is a system that distributes those feelings widely.

The essay responds by moving repeatedly from the “I” to the institution. A personal habit becomes a question about design. A private insecurity becomes a question about visibility and comparison. A moment of online pleasure becomes a question about the business model that makes the pleasure profitable. The movement keeps the individual experience vivid without treating it as sufficient explanation.

This is where the essay’s title becomes a formal principle. The “I” in the internet is not simply the narrator. It is a problem the narrator cannot solve by introspection. The self is shaped in relation to systems that record and respond to it. To understand the self, one must examine the environment that makes the self feel compelled to explain itself.

Tolentino’s prose combines cultural criticism with a controlled confessional voice. The tone can be witty, but the wit does not release the writer from the argument. It reveals the absurdity of trying to remain authentic inside a system that turns authenticity into content. The essay’s style mirrors its subject: it is alert to performance while depending on the reader’s sense of intimacy.
## Platforms and power

The essay’s political horizon is visible in its treatment of platform power. The user appears to have choice, but the choices are shaped by interfaces, defaults, rankings, and economic incentives. What becomes visible is not determined by personal merit alone. It is filtered through systems that decide what will be recommended, monetised, or suppressed.

This does not make users powerless. Tolentino’s argument is not technological determinism. People invent uses that platforms did not anticipate, build communities, and create forms of knowledge that established institutions would not provide. Yet the platform can absorb those inventions and turn them toward its own ends. Resistance may become a style, a brand, or another source of engagement.

The result is a culture in which the self is constantly negotiating between expression and capture. To speak is to risk being used. To remain silent is to lose access to the social and political possibilities of public presence. The essay does not offer a clean exit because the internet is no longer a detachable part of modern life. It is an environment through which work, friendship, politics, and identity are organised.

Tolentino’s contribution is to make that environment strange again. By describing familiar actions as problems of power, she interrupts the assumption that the feed is natural. The reader is asked to see design where there seemed to be convenience, labour where there seemed to be spontaneity, and economic interest where there seemed to be personal connection.
## The essay’s recursive form

“The I in the Internet” moves recursively. It begins with the self, turns toward the internet, then returns to the self as something altered by the encounter. This structure reflects the problem it analyses. The individual cannot be isolated from the medium, and the medium cannot be understood without the individual’s desires and habits.

The essay’s examples and reflections accumulate rather than establish a single causal proof. Tolentino is not writing a technical account of platform engineering or a complete history of the web. She is tracing a cultural condition through the feelings it produces and the forms of conduct it normalises. The essay’s evidence is therefore experiential and structural at once.

Its argumentative force comes from refusing the usual moral split between the innocent user and the corrupt corporation. The user may be exploited and still participate in exploitation. The platform may offer real connection and still organise that connection for profit. The critic may expose the system and still depend on the attention it generates. These contradictions are not flaws to be edited out. They are the conditions of contemporary digital life.

The personal essay is especially suited to this analysis because it can show how a system enters ordinary consciousness. A report can describe data extraction. A personal essay can show what it feels like to think of one’s own life as a stream of possible content. Tolentino’s form makes the political intimate without reducing politics to feeling.
## Living with the networked self

Tolentino does not promise that the self can be recovered in a pure state outside the internet. The task is not to discover an authentic identity untouched by media. There has never been a self without social form. The task is to notice how the current forms shape desire, attention, and memory, and to regain some capacity to judge those pressures.

That capacity may begin with refusing the story that online life is merely a private choice. A user can change habits, but the culture also requires collective decisions about labour, privacy, ownership, and public accountability. The individual solution is not enough because the problem is infrastructural. Yet individual awareness still matters because systems reproduce themselves through ordinary actions.

The essay’s tone remains ambivalent to the end. The internet is not an alien force imposed on passive users. It is a human construction that has become difficult to govern. Its pleasures are real, its possibilities are real, and its harms are real. Any serious criticism must hold all three facts together.

“The I in the Internet” leaves the reader with a self that is less private and less stable than it first appeared. The “I” is not erased by the network, but it is continually negotiated within it. To write about that condition is to ask whether a person can remain an agent while being watched, sorted, and encouraged to perform. Tolentino’s answer is cautious but not hopeless. Agency begins with making the structure visible, then deciding what forms of attention and relation are worth defending.
